items.title: arnaud behzadi on designing beyond beauty, from paris’ doobie’s to pavyllon lyon
items.summary:
the french architect discusses how memory, emotion, and hospitality shape two new restaurants, from a parisian icon to a culinary school in lyon. 
 The post  arnaud behzadi on designing beyond beauty, from paris’ doobie’s to pavyllon lyon  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] WHEN ARCHITECTURE LEARNS TO LISTEN Speaking with Arnaud Behzadi is something of a masterclass in understanding architecture beyond aesthetics. For the Paris-based architect, spaces are living entities, capable of provoking emotions, awakening memories, and shaping human relationships, provided they have been designed with enough sensitivity. His approach challenges the notion that beauty is something we merely observe. Instead, he believes it is something we experience, often without fully understanding why. This conviction runs through his work, from his furniture collection BAM to two of his latest hospitality projects: the reinvention of Doobie’s, an iconic Parisian restaurant , and Pavyllon Lyon, conceived in collaboration with celebrated chef Yannick Alléno. Although radically different in character and purpose, both reveal an architect determined to create places that resonate long after the first impression has faded. For Behzadi, architecture begins with an exercise that might sound deceptively simple: listening. ‘We learn at school to listen, to hear, not so much to watch the space,’ he tells designboom, describing a process of observing materials, light, emptiness, and the sensations they produce before drawing a single line. Only then does he establish what he calls a narrative program, a conceptual thread that informs every subsequent decision. This philosophy finds an especially personal expression at Doobie’s , located at 26 Rue Marbeuf in Paris’ eighth arrondissement. Founded in 1938, the establishment became a fixture of Parisian nightlife in the 1990s, a place Behzadi himself remembers from his younger years. Following three years of transformation, the architect has given it a second life without attempting to erase its first. ‘What I remember more than everything was the energy of this place,’ he recalls. ‘I was really feeling that I was being hosted, that I was home, not that I was being served.’ warm, intimate interiors at Doobie’s | images by Amaury Laparra unless otherwise stated ARNAUD BEHZADI BREATHES NEW LIFE INTO DOOBIE’S IN PARIS Rather than designing another fashionable restaurant, Behzadi drew inspiration from the tradition of Parisian private dinners, where artists, politicians, writers, and intellectuals would gather around the same table. He studied the domestic worlds of figures such as the Agnellis, François Catroux, and Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, imagining Doobie’s as the home of a fictional couple whose possessions and memories have accumulated over generations. The result unfolds through a succession of intimate rooms: the Grand Salon, a velvet-lined rotunda, the Petit Salon, the Retour de Voyage, and an unexpected indoor garden beneath a glass roof. Mahogany, stained oak, dark marble, lacquered surfaces, and warm lighting establish an atmosphere that feels deliberately lived-in. Artworks, selected through visits to galleries and discoveries made during Behzadi’s travels, reinforce this impression. ‘I did it as a home, not as a restaurant,’ he explains, emphasizing that each object was chosen with the same instinct he would apply to his own living space. Curiously, the project’s extended development became one of its greatest advantages. Structural complications delayed construction by several months, allowing Behzadi to revisit decisions and refine details that might otherwise have remained unresolved. The design now extends to the smallest architectural gestures, including the nocturnal bar with its lacquered mahogany and mirrored ceiling, and the downstairs washrooms, where artist Dominic J. Masullo has created a painted scene inspired by classical antiquity. For Behzadi, these interventions are meaningful only when they contribute to the larger narrative. ‘All the details have to have sense and meaning,’ he insists. He recalls overhearing two guests discussing the restaurant shortly after its reopening. Unaware that the architect was standing nearby, they remarked that whoever designed the place had clearly put his heart into it. It was, perhaps, a more meaningful compliment than any architectural review. 1/9 PAVYLLON LYON TURNS HOSPITALITY INTO A LESSON Some 460 kilometers southeast of Paris, Behzadi’s approach takes on an entirely different dimension at Pavyllon Lyon, the restaurant opened in September 2026 by Yannick Alléno and Institut Lyfe. Situated on Place Bellecour, the project is the world’s first Pavyllon restaurant-school, welcoming the public while providing approximately 600 students each year with practical experience alongside professional chefs and hospitality teams. Here, architecture must do considerably more than impress diners: it must also support an educational mission. ‘Hospitality is first an emotion, not beauty,’ Behzadi explains, recalling the moment he watched the students enter the completed restaurant for the first time. Their excitement moved him profoundly, confirming that the atmosphere he had sought to create was being experienced by the very people This respect for authenticity becomes particularly important in a restaurant where the next generation of hospitality professionals is learning its craft. Rather than surrounding students with ostentatious luxury, Behzadi envisioned an environment that could communicate the values of French hospitality through proportion, materiality, and atmosphere. The dining room becomes a stage, with guests observing the movements of chefs and students, while the architecture quietly supports their interaction. ‘We were very aligned on not going too much into luxury. And if it’s luxury, it has to be very calm,’ he explains. The project’s success, in his view, has little to do with spectacular architectural gestures. What matters is the energy that emerges when people occupy the space, interact with one another, and feel comfortable enough to make it their own. 1/3 photographer: Ambroise Tézenas photographer: Ambroise Tézenas photographer: Ambroise Tézenas WH

items.title: terracotta tones and botanical palettes define line arc’s hospitality-infused offices in almaty
items.summary:
blending warm modernism, bespoke regional craftsmanship, and kazakh cultural motifs, the flexible layout pairs open coworking hubs with private suites and a central social café. 
 The post  terracotta tones and botanical palettes define line arc’s hospitality-infused offices in almaty  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] LINE ARC develops HOSPITALITY-INFUSED ESENTAI OFFICES in ALMATY Completed in 2025 within the Esentai Apartments complex in Almaty, Kazakhstan, Esentai Offices is a 984.91-sqm workplace designed by Line Arc under the direction of principal designer Ilnara Seitzhanova. Moving away from conventional corporate layouts, the single-level plan integrates hospitality-driven interiors, flexible coworking zones, and regional craftsmanship. all images ©Damir Otegen RE-ENGINEERED framework FREES PLAN FOR PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ZONES Before addressing finishes, the design team selectively demolished and re-engineered dense overhead MEP infrastructure and an existing water-based fire suppression network to preserve ceiling heights. Integrated lighting systems by Aledo and Flua were paired with zoned HVAC distribution to maintain uniform air exchange and tailored illumination. Spatially, the floor plan separates public amenities from private workspaces: the communal zone comprises an entrance lobby, lounges, a central café with a back-of-house kitchen, a 40-seat auditorium, modular conference rooms, a speaker tribune, recreation areas, and a sleep capsule. In contrast, the private wing houses scalable suites accommodating two to 23 workstations, executive offices, print hubs, and kitchenettes, bordered by integrated indoor greenhouses and outdoor terraces. bespoke terracotta shelves and natural wood paneling display curated ceramics BOTANICAL PALETTES and CERAMIC SCONCES REFERENCE KAZAKH CRAFT The material palette draws its chromatic cues from botanical Italian wall coverings in the lounge, establishing a muted register of terracotta, olive, pastel blue, and sand. Vertical decorative plaster by Gris Design forms a textured perimeter, paired with 1524×228 mm Enviro quartz-vinyl planks in main circulation routes and acoustic carpeting by Bloq and Clerkenwell inside meeting rooms. Kazakh cultural references are integrated through contemporary craft rather than literal motifs, including hand-molded ceramic sconces by local artisans, regional desk seating shaped after the silhouette of the traditional dombra and upholstered in Italian textiles, a felt wall installation by Laila Zharkyn, and original tapestries by Malik Mukanov. custom artwork by Malik Mukanov integrates Kazakh textile heritage into the modern workspace Esentai Offices’ flexible workplace pairs re-engineered infrastructure with Kazakh art natural veneer paneling creates intricate curvature metallic wall finishes contrast with warm wood detailing and plush terracotta upholstery the lounge area pairs botanical-patterned Italian wall coverings with soft curved seating the junction of wood and metal balances tactile materiality with sleek architectural lines View this post on Instagram A post shared by ByStorm (@by.strm) the central social café serves as the main social hub of Esentai Offices the central social café features stainless steel counters and custom seating the central café and lounge hub anchors the public zone, encouraging informal collaboration the single-level floor plan replaces standard corporate cubicles with a hospitality-oriented layout custom seating crafted by local artisans echoes the curved silhouette of the traditional Kazakh dombra a muted palette of terracotta, olive, pastel blue, and sand defines the interiors project info: name: Esentai Offices architect: Line Arc lead designer: Ilnara Seitzhanova location: Almaty, Kazakhstan photographer: Damir Otegen designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. items.title: hyan adapts 1970s timber frame into live-work residence on the hills of hayama
items.summary:
the existing columns and beams are retained and structurally strengthened, while the interior is reorganized around a double-height living room and a recessed doma created from a former tatami room. 
 The post  hyan adapts 1970s timber frame into live-work residence on the hills of hayama  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] HYAN SEISMICALLY RETROFITS AND REMODELS 1970S TIMBER RESIDENCE Located in a hillside residential district of Hayama, Kanagawa, Japan , Green Sandwich House is the adaptive reuse of a late-1970s timber residence converted into a combined home and studio for architect Anna Naganuma and designer Shohei Hasegawa of Japanese architecture practice HYAN. Rather than demolishing the pre-1981 seismic-code structure, the studio retained the undamaged timber columns and beams, integrated seismic reinforcements, and reconfigured the interior layout to support overlapping domestic and studio functions. Green Sandwich House is a renovated 1970s timber residence in Hayama | all images ©Katsuhiro Aoki DOUBLE-HEIGHT LIVING ROOM AND RECESSED DOMA ORGANIZE OPEN PLAN Studio HYAN anchors the ground floor around a central double-height living room that connects the kitchen, pantry, study, garden, and a newly formed doma. Carved from a former tatami room by removing the traditional matting and altering the floor elevation, the doma incorporates a converted closet nook to serve as a multi-purpose threshold for working, hosting, and lounging. Instead of relying on solid partitions, the floor plan delineates programmatic zones through changes in floor level, sightlines, material transitions, and movable textiles. Custom curtains designed by textile artist Haruka Shoji frame the large openings and the doma, filtering daylight and garden views throughout the day. New functional surfaces, including the kitchen countertops and washbasin, are finished in hand-ground, in-situ terrazzo, establishing a tactile contrast against the exposed, aged timber frame. a double-height living room anchors the ground floor, promoting natural ventilation and light distribution large glazed openings visually extend the central living space toward the surrounding greenery original structural columns and ceiling beams are retained and left exposed throughout the interior the kitchen island and counters are finished in terrazzo that contrasts with the warm timber frame detail view showing the aggregate texture of the cast-in-place terrazzo worktop against wooden joinery a custom washbasin in matching hand-ground terrazzo maintains material continuity across wet zones custom curtains act as permeable partitions that modulate light and garden views a former tatami room turns into a recessed doma by stripping the matting and adjusting floor levels the double-height living volume preserves acoustic and visual connection across floors the upper floor tile-clad bathroom overlooks the surrounding hillside views the renovation demonstrates an incremental approach to updating Japan’s aging residential housing 1/2 plan section project info: name: Green Sandwich House / A 1970s House Renovation architect: HYAN | @hyan_studio lead architect: Anna Naganuma lead designer: Shohei Hasegawa construction: Deguchi Tategu-ten textiles: Haruka Shoji location: Hayama, Kanagawa, Japan site area: 271.18 sqm floor area: 106.2 sqm photographer: Katsuhiro Aoki | @katsuhiroaoki designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. items.title: HUSTLR Pickleball & Social Club / CYS Architect Sdn Bhd
items.summary: An abandoned food court in Taman Taynton View, Cheras, has been transformed into Hustlr Pickleball & Social Club — a new sports and social destination that adapts an existing steel structure while introducing a distinctive identity and a new layer of community life. What can an underutilized building become when its potential is reconsidered? For Hustlr, the answer was not to start again, but to work with what was already there. Inspired by the client's passion for pickleball, the vision extended beyond creating a place to play.

items.title: Sona Listening Practices / Épico Studio
items.summary: Sona is a space dedicated to listening practices, designed by Épico Estudio and Panorama. Located in the heart of  Mexico City , in the Condesa neighborhood, the 245 m² venue—spearheaded by a group of friends led by Luis López (Lulo)—is defined as an environment oriented toward sonic immersion: device-free, alcohol-free, and distraction-free. The concept transforms the act of listening into a conscious, deliberate, shared, and, above all, deeply sensory experience.

items.title: ROOM’s Designers on Design Series Returns with A Story of Hospitality and Human Connection
items.summary: In the latest episode, industry icon Anda Andrei and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich discuss the ups and downs of hospitality design, creative inspirations, and more
items.text: Partner Content ROOM’s Designers on Design Series Returns with A Story of Hospitality and Human Connection 11.12.26 | By Design Milk Staff Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM. Who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer? That’s the core concept behind ROOM ’s Designers on Design video series, which pairs leading designers together for open conversation on the future of architecture, design, and human connection. “When we launched ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” says Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM. “No interviewer, no moderator, no prescribed talking points. Just two creative minds coming together to exchange ideas, challenge perspectives, and explore what moves the industry forward.” Hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation. Unlike earlier episodes of this series, Andrei and Goodrich know each other outside of the studio—and have for years. Goodrich attributes his love of hospitality design to Andrei’s hotels, while Andrei has had a front-row seat to the evolution of Goodrich’s career. (Plus, their work shares a certain symbiosis: Andrei’s recent renovation of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris aligns with Goodrich’s past in museum exhibition design.) “For this episode, we wanted to take a slightly different approach to our previous pairings,” says Heckman. “Rather than bringing together designers who may be meeting for the first time, we were drawn to the idea of connecting two individuals who already share a history and familiarity with each other’s work. We loved the opportunity to explore how those relationships shape our perspectives, influence our creative instincts and ultimately help us grow as designers.” Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM. Tapping into the spirit of authentic exchange that ROOM set out to foster, the duo’s conversation begins with their first (almost) meeting. In 2003, Goodrich was helping his partner, Barnes Foundation Executive Director Thomas Collins, open Zaha Hadid’s Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati when he heard that Andrei would be there in 20 minutes. “I looked to Thom, and I said, ‘You’ve got to go home, take a shower, and put on a suit. This is a big deal,’” Goodrich shares. However, the pair didn’t officially meet until years later—after Andrei had left the Ian Schrager Company, starting her own firm at 59 years old. “You came very highly recommended, and I wanted to hire you,” she says. “But then I asked you a crucial question: ‘Have you ever opened a hotel before?’” “And I had to say no,” Goodrich adds. Designing a hotel is no easy feat, which Goodrich learned when opening his first hotel, Arlo SoHo, in 2016. He shared how the final month before opening was chaos. With nearly 40 years shaping hospitality projects, Andrei knows this reality well—but emphasizes that it’s even more painful when operations start changing after the design is finished. Like living organisms, hospitality projects evolve with the staff, users, and guests over the years. Still, the pair agree that all these issues and pain points provide valuable lessons. “Understanding how operations affect the success of restaurants and of hotels is foundational for making great designs,” Goodrich says. Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM. On the topic of design inspiration, Andrei believe the best hotels have a story. Much like an elevator pitch, she believes projects should have a one-sentence design concept. For example, at the Delano Miami Beach Hotel, which she created in collaboration with Philippe Starck, the one-liner was: “a Greek fisherman that finds a diamond in the sea.” Goodrich agrees with the sentiment of this design tool: “If you have that short phrase, if you can go back to the essence of what your concept is, things fall into place.” Throughout the episode, there is a sense of mutual respect and deep appreciation for the other’s work. Goodrich calls Andrei a superhero collaborator, while Andrei compliments Goodrich’s work (and name). Both value collaboration, imagination, and challenging work. Heckman sees the pair’s connection as proof of the series’ larger purpose: “It’s a wonderful example of how seemingly different creative paths can intersect, and how the work we encounter early in our careers can continue to influence us in unexpected ways.” “When you started your company, we had some empty desks in my office and we shared offices. And who knew that nine and a half years later, we would be sitting here and talking about how amazing you did,” Andrei says with a laugh. This is what ROOM’s Designers on Design series does so well: It brings design to the human level. From the ideas and experiences that shape the work to the friends, colleagues, and mentors who leave a lasting impact, each episode looks at the people behind the portfolio. “What makes this episode especially compelling is that the conversation extends beyond design itself,” shares Heckman. “It gets to the heart of how we become the designers we are — the people who influence us, the experiences that shape our creative instincts, and the ways inspiration gets passed from one generation to the next. In that sense, it embodies exactly what we hoped the series would become: a platform for authentic exchange, unexpected perspectives and the stories behind the work.” And who knows? The series might even inspire new work of its own. “I want to do a project together,” Andrei says. Goodrich answers: “I know, me too. That’s my dream.” Watch the episode at room.com Now Trending Partner Content Partner Content Walnut and Leather Meet at the Seams of Eureka Ergonomic’s Arundel Collecti

items.title: Neri&Hu Reinterprets Cape Town’s Maritime Heritage for Edition
items.summary: Industrial architecture, locally sourced materials, and South African craftsmanship create a contemporary hotel rooted in the city’s waterfront history
items.text: Travel Neri&Hu Reinterprets Cape Town’s Maritime Heritage for Edition 11.12.26 | By Malia Agostinelli Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow The Cape Town Edition, designed by Neri&Hu, draws on the industrial maritime heritage of the city’s V&A Waterfront. Photography by Jiri Lizler. Neri&Hu Reinterprets Cape Town’s Maritime Heritage for Edition Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 2/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 3/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 4/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 5/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 6/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 7/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 8/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 9/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 10/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 11/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 12/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 13/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 14/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 15/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 16/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 17/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 18/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 19/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 20/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 21/22 Photos Photography by Jiri Lizler 22/22 Photos The Cape Town Edition, designed by Neri&Hu, draws on the industrial maritime heritage of the city’s V&A Waterfront. Photography by Jiri Lizler. Located on Quay 7 at the V&A Waterfront in Cape Town, South Africa, the Cape Town Edition Hotel turns heritage into a destination that feels contemporary yet unmistakably local. Designed by Neri&Hu in partnership with local architects and professional firms, the hotel draws inspiration from the site’s industrial maritime character while embracing the city’s evolving cultural landscape. Although the original warehouse was too unstable to preserve, its footprint and construction logic informed the new building, which references the long, narrow forms and pitched roofs of the surrounding industrial structures. Photography by Jiri Lizler Part of a global portfolio of hotels, The Cape Town Edition revolves around The Drum—a soaring cylindrical space open to the elements. The harbor, Table Mountain, the Atlantic, and the waterfront below are all visible from the 360-degree outdoor viewing platform. Guests, visitors, and locals alike can ascend the spiral staircase to discover Cape Town from a bird’s-eye view. Photography by Jiri Lizler For Lyndon Neri , co-founder of Neri&Hu, The Drum began with a conversation about how to connect and distinguish the hotel’s hospitality and residential spaces. “The route is both architectural and civic,” he says. “It turns circulation into an experience of the landscape and gives the project a public dimension beyond accommodation.” Photography by Jiri Lizler Grounded in its landscape, the Cape Town Edition is crafted with a deep appreciation for materiality. Local sourcing was central to the hotel’s sustainability strategy, informing not only the selection of building materials but also the curation of the furniture, art, and objects throughout the space. Photography by Jiri Lizler Metalwork and joinery were supplied by local manufacturers, while the joinery draws inspiration from 19th-century travel trunks. Custom furnishings manufactured locally and rugs woven by KwaZulu-Natal-based Shuttleworth Weaving layer exceptional craftsmanship into the interiors, where warm finishes are complemented by expansive window frames that capture sweeping views. Photography by Jiri Lizler More than 6 million bricks, supplied by a family-owned Western Cape manufacturer and laid by hand, create shifting patterns across the façade, giving the building texture and rhythm. Their warm sand tones complement the natural hues of the surrounding landscape, providing a striking backdrop against the cooler blues of the sea beyond. Photography by Jiri Lizler “Our interest was never in an architecture that competes with this landscape, nor one that simply defers to it,” Neri says. “Instead, we asked how the building might register those forces: how brick, light, and the deliberate framing of views could create a sequence of spaces at once bound to the Waterfront and unmistakably of Cape Town.” Photography by Jiri Lizler Throughout the hotel, art serves a purpose beyond decoration, reflecting Africa’s creative landscape and connecting guests to the people and traditions that shape the destination. Design Network Africa sourced objects from makers across the continent, including Zulu ukhamba vessels and mouth-blown recycled glass from Eswatini. Cape Town gallery Southern Guild curated the art collection, which includes black-and-white portraits by Zanele Muholi, Usha Seejarim’s artwork Fading Dish Cloth , and smoke-fired ceramics by Chuma Maweni, which lend a sculptural presence to the lobby and dining spaces. Photography by Jiri Lizler A 240-square-meter Penthouse and a 112-square-meter Harbor Suite crown the hotel, each offering ample living spaces and panoramic views. The Cape Town Edition comprises 142 guestrooms and suites that balance elevated comfort with residential appeal. Below sea level, the spa features a sauna, steam room, infrared beds, and aromatherapy. A daily program of sound baths, yoga classes, and movement sessions enhances the experience, with additional opportunities to unwind beside the heated rooftop pool and sundeck. Photography by Jiri Lizler The Punch Room draws on the centuries-old tradition of communal punch drinking, a ritual carried along trade routes that once passed through the Cape. Velvet banquettes, wood paneling, and atmospheric lighting create an opulent retreat that offers a modern interpretation of the region’s rich cultural and culinary heritage. Photography by Jiri Lizler The end goal? For guests and visitors to leave with a lasting sense of Cape Town, shaped by the connections between the hotel’s interiors and the surroundi

items.title: At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden  
  At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: At water level: inside Magma's Sauna Garden • Hotel Designs At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 16, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden In the Catalan spa town of Santa Coloma de Farners, INBECA has designed, built and installed one of the largest Finnish saunas in Europe – a ninety-square-metre landscape of wood, glass and heat with a garden at its heart… Magma is a thermal spa fed by natural mineral waters, the very origin of wellness culture. Its latest chapter is OASI, a sensory space conceived as a journey through heat, salt, steam and cold. At its centre sits the Sauna Garden, created by INBECA, the Barcelona-based wellness manufacturer that has been crafting saunas and steam rooms since 1964. Image credit: David Rueda / Magma Centre Lúdic Termal A sauna that unfolds like a landscape With a floor plan of 9.42 × 9.54 metres, the Sauna Garden is less a cabin than a place to wander. Two-tier semicircular benches in hemlock trace soft curves around an indoor garden, while curved glass lets the planting and the light flow through the space. LED lines beneath the benches lift the light from the floor, and chromotherapy glows behind the backrests. Four concealed heaters create different zones between 75 and 90 °C, so each guest can find their own intensity. Every element was made to measure. Three of the four doors are accessible, the bench fronts can be removed for maintenance, and the whole sauna is managed through INBECA’s Ecotouch control system – details that rarely make the photographs, yet shape how a space like this performs day after day. Image credit: David Rueda / Magma Centre Lúdic Termal Salt, steam and a vault of black Beyond the sauna, the journey continues. A 2.24 m² wall of salt blocks glows from within, washing the room in warm tones. In the hammam, a vaulted black acrylic ceiling turns the steam dense and silent above a U-shaped bench for up to twelve people. The 7.07 × 5.36 metre cabin was adapted to the building’s existing pillars, with a vaulted niche housing two black Bossini showers and a basin with an integrated tap. Image credit: David Rueda / Magma Centre Lúdic Termal The moment the water falls Contrast is part of the ritual. In three tall, narrow cabins bathed in blue, a single pull on a handle releases thirty litres of water from a stainless-steel bucket. The journey ends with cold: ice falls into an illuminated glass bowl, waiting for a hand to gather it. Image credit: David Rueda / Magma Centre Lúdic Termal Made for the space, not the catalogue For INBECA, Magma illustrates a way of working that runs through its projects for hotels, spas and sports clubs: bespoke design, in-house manufacturing and integration into existing architecture. Four generations on, the family company has delivered wellness spaces in more than 30 countries. “A garden embraces the wood and glass; inside, the heat waits at water level.” This article is part of our paid content offering. To explore sponsored editorial opportunities with Hotel Designs please contact Katy Phillips. items.title: In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN  
  In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN • Hotel Designs In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 16, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN AKAN is a family-owned collection of distinctive hotels, all of which share a common thread of Moroccan heritage, generosity and connection – we spoke to Youssef Benabbès Tâarji to find out how the brand is shaping a new chapter in Moroccan hospitality… Following on from the recent El Fenn Review, we spoke to Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, Co-Founder and Head of Development and Asset Management at AKAN, to gain a little more insight into what it means to bring a new perspective to a legacy built over three generations. We explore how the group is protecting the spirit of El Fenn and the other distinctive properties in its portfolio, while defining what comes next for the brand. Image credit: Villa des Orangers Hotel Designs: AKAN is a family-led brand – can you tell us a little about the story behind the brand and how does that sense of family influence the way you build the business? Youssef Benabbès Tâarji: Both Marrakech and hotels have been in my family for generations. My great great grandfather was Marrakchi and my grandfather Ahmed was born in the medina in the 1930s. In fact, he grew up only a few streets from what is now El Fenn and became one of the pioneers of Moroccan tourism when he co-founded Holidays Services in 1973. My father Jalil then built our family’s hotel group over the following decades and AKAN is the third act, my chapter, alongside my cousin Malika, who is AKAN’s CFO. Three generations of one family, three movements of the same engagement: to receive people in our country as one opens one’s home. The story of the three houses reflects that approach. It took my father just three minutes to answer an email about the possible sale of La Villa des Orangers. We hadn’t even looked at a spreadsheet but it was pure emotional recognition. We knew Les Deux Tours for years because my grandparents live nearby in the Palmeraie and had made it one of their favourite places to dine long before it became ours. And El Fenn is a house every Marrakchi knows by name, a landmark in the city we grew up in. Each acquisition was less a deal than a homecoming. That family dimension shapes everything. We are building something to last for the next generation, not a portfolio to trade. Our teams are treated as part of the household too. Many of them have been with our houses for more than two decades. Image credit: Villa des Orangers HD: There is something inherently personal about a family-built hospitality brand. How important is that sense of personal connection to the way AKAN operates? YBT: I think personal connection is what transforms any brand from surface-level to one that goes far deeper – and that’s what people connect to. In a world of slick marketing and messaging, people can feel when something has true depth. So for us, AKAN isn’t just a brand. It is a collection of singular houses, each one reflecting different facets of Morocco. Our teams are largely Moroccan, they work in houses that celebrate their own culture, under owners who are themselves Moroccan. There is a different kind of engagement that comes from that, and guests feel it even when they cannot name it. The most meaningful part of a stay is not always what happens inside the walls. It’s important of course but so too are the moments when a guests connects outside the hotel to the living culture around them – meeting a master ceramicist and watching them turn a piece of clay, sitting with the women of a Berber embroidery collective, crossing paths with an artist in residence at El Fenn. Those encounters are only possible because our teams are of this place, and because we know these makers personally. Hospitality, for us, begins with opening the door to the people who make Morocco what it is. El Fenn | Image credit: Moggi Photography HD: How do you define the difference between an AKAN hotel and simply a hotel that happens to be in Morocco? YBT: There is a very Moroccan reflex I recognise in myself and in almost everyone I know. When a friend from abroad says they are coming to visit, we all quietly turn into ambassadors for our own country. We start drawing up an itinerary, this workshop, that terrace at sunset, this friend who weaves, that maker who should not be missed. We cannot help it. It is genuine pride, and it is generosity in its most Moroccan form. That same impulse is behind AKAN. Our guests are received as friends we want to share the country with, with insider access to the traditions, ateliers and communities they could not find on their own. Each of our three houses offers something different. At El Fenn, it’s art, design and the energy of the medina. Les Deux Tours offers architecture, nature and wellness rituals in a quieter part of Marrakech. La Villa des Orangers holds the classical traditions of Marrakchi hospitality, with gastronomy and craft at its centre. The common thread however is that we are not interpreting Morocco from the outside. This is our home. The Morocco we share is for the curious, from those who live it. HD: What are the values that you want every AKAN property to share, regardless of where it is or what it looks like? YBT: Four values run through all our houses: rooted in place, human at heart, generous in spirit, and a role as tastemakers and curators. Rooted in place means each house speaks its own geography and its own history. We do not import a signature. Human at heart is expressed in the way our teams work and the way guests are received. Generous in spirit is the one I hold closest. We champion the artisans, artists and makers who made Marrakech what it is, not only the houses we own. items.text: Inside ŪRJĀ, the Maldives’ new naturopathy island Healing by design: inside ŪRJĀ, the Maldives’ new naturopathy island WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 13, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Healing by design: inside ŪRJĀ, the Maldives’ new naturopathy island Over-water suites, open-air rituals and the pulse of the Indian Ocean set the scene at ŪRJĀ, the new Naturopathy Island at Four Seasons Maldives at Kuda Huraa, where ancient healing meets modern science… Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Kuda Huraa has recently unveiled ŪRJĀ Naturopathy Island, the next evolution of holistic healing in the Maldives. Named after the Sanskrit word for vitality, ŪRJĀ is a wellness destination with a difference. Its programme balances naturopathic principles with scientific expertise, shifting the focus from surface-level relaxation to meaningful restoration. ŪRJĀ was created with a clear intention: to move beyond the sameness of many modern spa experiences and offer something deeper. A space where ancient knowledge, natural healing and personal empowerment come together in harmony. Beyond buzzwords, trends and quick fixes, ŪRJĀ is designed for genuine, ongoing healing, not momentary escape. Image credit: Four Seasons Resorts Many treatments at ŪRJĀ feature AION A, the powerful healing mineral discovered in an ancient Roman quarry in Würenlos, Switzerland by visionary Swiss naturopathic researcher Emma Kunz (1892–1963). Named after the Greek for ‘without limitation’, AION A supports detoxification, soothes inflammation and encourages healing via positively charged ion exchange. Rather than chasing the latest wellness protocol, ŪRJĀ takes a holistic path rooted in knowledge, education and integrity. In a world defined by stress, digital overwhelm and physical fatigue, it asks: what do guests truly need now? The answer is timeless: naturopathy, practising for centuries what the modern world now calls ‘biohacking’, restores balance, supports natural healing and guides enduring, sustainable habits. Rooted in this philosophy, ŪRJĀ’s programmes unite nutrition, movement, detoxification and energetic realignment, for lasting wellbeing. The imparting of knowledge is central to the experience. Guests learn about the body’s innate intelligence, the importance of rhythm and nourishment, and how small, consistent changes can restore vitality. Diagnostics, consultations and personalised guidance empower them to return home with deeper understanding and practical tools for everyday wellbeing. ŪRJĀ’s philosophy also recognises the growing need for stillness. In a world of constant stimulation, moments of silence and reflection become powerful therapeutic tools. Experiences encourage guests to reconnect with nature, their breath and the peace found within. Image credit: Four Season Resorts Accessed from the resort’s main jetty via a small Maldivian dhoni, ŪRJĀ offers a deep immersion in elemental rhythms, a living reflection of its ethos of vitality through nature. Over-water treatment suites, open-air rituals and the pulse of the surrounding ocean immerse guests in natural rejuvenation. The spa’s pioneering approach centres on individualised wellness. At its heart are four core naturopathic pathways: Rest & Rebalance, Cleanse, Nourish and Reconnect. Each pathway offers a collection of therapies and rituals to align mind, body, emotions and intellect, awakening self-healing. Every journey begins with an expert Naturopathic Consultation to craft a bespoke programme of therapeutic care. Optional micronutrient scans, iris diagnosis and postural mapping offer deeper insight into internal balance and vitality. Signature treatments include Mud Therapy, Heliotherapy, Life-Force Healing, Magneto Therapy and Sound Healing. Complementing these are Yoga Therapy, and traditional naturopathic practices such as fasting, acupuncture and full-body alignment rituals. Highlights include the ‘Vagus Reset’, a centring ritual that activates the vagus nerve, and the Night Spa Ritual, a celestial open-air experience aligned with the rhythms of the cosmos. ŪRJĀ also offers specialised programmes guided by the team of onsite Naturopathic Doctors to address root causes of imbalance through therapies, coaching and nutrition. From Sleep Enhancement to Liver Detox and Joint Care, each is designed to restore and sustain lasting health. ŪRJĀ’s approach is complemented by the work of visionary Swiss naturopath and artist Emma Kunz. Four Seasons has exclusive access to Kunz’s geometric drawings, believed to emit healing energy and reflect universal principles, which illustrate ŪRJĀ’s treatment menu. items.title: Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech  
  Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech • Hotel Designs Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 13, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech It’s not just oud and orange blossom that perfume the courtyards of El Fenn, as Digital Editor Pauline Brettell discovered – those bold red walls are all bound together by the heady fragrance of collaboration and team spirit… Having been offered the opportunity for a ‘first-look’ at the reimagined rooms at El Fenn , I hastily booked my El Boraq ticket, packed my bags and headed south on the fast-train to explore the hotel’s trademark Moroccan maximalism. El Fenn is, quite frankly, the original Grande Dame of cool in Marrakech . Over the years, under the leadership of Vanessa Branson, it has been a leading light in this city of oh-so-many sparkling lights and mysterious lanterns. Vanessa Branson remains integrally involved as a brand ambassador, continuing to champion the spirit of creativity and collaboration that has always set the hotel apart. Recently the Branson leadership baton has passed to AKAN which, in its own words, is ‘a collection of unmatched properties ’. Together with La Villa des Orangers and Les Deux Tours, El Fenn completes the picture , and the updates and additions of the new guestrooms, are simply a new thread adding another layer to the consistently colourful story of the riad. Image credit: Moggi Studio After an evening that started on the iconic red-and-white-striped rooftop terrace, I ended my day cocooned in layers of colour and texture, pattern and patina in a gloriously generous, double-aspect (a luxury in itself) guestroom, framed by dramatic black tadelakt walls. Gold leaf, vintage lights and a bathroom bigger than many a hotel guestroom, all surrounded the statement Moroccan four poster bed, making it a hard call to get up in the morning. Image credit: El Fenn But get up I did, as I was woken by the transportive sound of birdsong and fountains. After a little luxurious hammam-style shower time, I headed back up to the terrace to start the day with strong coffee and a slow breakfast. Adequately fortified, wandered down to the central courtyard of the riad, marveling at evry design detail along the way, to meet Yann Dobry, Creative Director and Force behind El Fenn’s bold design footprint. I was also scheduled, a little later in the morning, to meet Hadia Temli, Curator and Gallerist of two Marrakech galleries – Galerie SINIYA28 and Galerie Tindouf – who facilitated the recent Rita Alaoui installation that greets you as you step into the hotel. Instead, in that aforementioned team spirit of brand El Fenn, meetings overlapped, mutual connections were discovered, stylish shopping tips exchanged, in a conversation punctuated by designers popping out from the boutique to ask for outfit opinions – it was far more interesting, a lot more fun, and aptly in the spirit of a place where the conversation between design and art is constantly in dialogue. Image credit: Moggi Studio A particular painting in the impressive hotel art collection can be the starting point for an entire room design. A colour from the palette, is then used to drench the walls in the textured traditional plaster, which in turn, can inform the choice of a handwoven Moroccan carpet, often another work of art in its own right. As we walked and talked our way around the hotel, we stepped inside the new-look ‘Cosy Rooms’ , which were preparing to receive their first guests. It felt a bit like being inside one of those kaleidoscopes I had as a kid: every turn of the dial shifted the glass prisms into another configuration of colour, light and pattern. In these reimagined guestrooms of El Fenn, the dimensions and colours create a strong and contained frame for all the details that make the whole. As different as they are, each with its own visual identity and story to tell, there is a strong visual thread that Yann has woven into the project – a particular intensity that draws everything together. Image credit: Moggi Studio The newly decorated rooms were originally part of a separate house, Vanessa’s riad, which was connected to the hotel. These four rooms have now been integrated into the property, both in terms of space and design. The rooms are characterised by big, bold gestures and colours. There is no sense of going small to fit the space; instead, the space is given a sense of opulence through scale. “People often think they have to shrink everything to fit smaller spaces, and that’s a mistake,” explained Dobry. “I wanted to create a kind of tension in these rooms because they are among our smaller spaces, and I very intentionally wanted to amplify that feeling by adding oversized art, as well as large headboards and upholstered pieces.” It is interesting how calm these rooms feel, despite the potentially busy layers of colour and pattern. Somehow, Yann has managed to create a conversation between big personalities rather than a competition. The headboards become works of art; the art becomes part of the design. Image credit: Moggi Studio Beyond the bedrooms, the conversation continued with Hadia talking us through another recent addition to the hotel: the Rita Alaoui project, which celebrates and continues El Fenn’s commitment to art and its community, as it transitions from Vanessa Branson’s very personal art haven to the AKAN Collection of boutique hotels. Long before the role of art in hotel design became a topic for panel discussions, El Fenn was already headlining its art collection and collaborations as part of the design story. items.title: Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels
items.summary:

 Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels  
  Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels  
 Sophie Harper .
items.text: Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels • Hotel Designs Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels WORDS BY Sophie Harper November 12, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels In the summer, Hotel Designs and Lutron hosted a group of hospitality and design specialists at The Chancery Rosewood to discuss what it really takes to turn a building with a past, into a hotel with a future… Manor houses, castles and former manufacturing plants all hold the potential to become extraordinary hotels. But transforming a building with a rich history into a contemporary hospitality destination requires more than an appreciation of its architecture. There are heritage restrictions to navigate, commercial realities to address and the expectations of a modern guest to consider. Above all, there is the challenge of introducing a new purpose without losing the character that made the building special in the first place. At this Hotel Designs roundtable, held in association with Lutron at the beautiful new The Chancery Rosewood in Mayfair, the panel sat down together to discuss the complexities of adaptive reuse from their own design experiences. From identifying a building’s potential and negotiating the demands of heritage conservation to integrating technology and building meaningful connections with local communities, the conversation considered what it takes to approach transformation layer by layer. On the panel Image credit: Photographer London Around the table were (pictured left to right, top to bottom): Paul Gallacher, Design Director at EPR Architects ; Natalia Miyar, Founder, Natalia Miyar ; Kim Partridge, Founder of Kim Partridge Interiors ; Nick de Klerk, Associate Partner & Head of Hotels, Purcell ; Despina Kalapoda, Senior Director Design Strategies EMEA, Marriott International ; Nicolla Farry, Hospitality Sales Manager UK & Ireland, Lutron ; Jessica Morrison, Design Director at GA ; Maria Wojtowicz, Head of Creative at Omnam ; and Sophie Harper, Editor, Hotel Designs. Finding the potential Every successful conversion starts with understanding what is already there. Beyond the obvious architectural features, it is the proportions, spatial relationships and underlying structure of a building that can determine whether it has the potential to work as a hotel. But even the most beautiful building needs to make sense operationally and commercially. Sophie Harper: When you first walk into a historic building earmarked for hotel conversion, what tells you it has ‘good bones’? And what are the warning signs that a project might be more trouble than it’s worth? Kim Partridge: I think, first of all, it’s instinct. We’ve all been in the business for a long time, so we develop that instinct – you’ll know quite quickly whether the bones are good. Proportion is really important, but one of the things we look for is fluidity. It has to flow and work properly. You cannot have this horrible overlap between the guest experience and staff and back of house. Maria Wojtowicz: For us, there are no red flags, per se. We’re very solution-focused and believe we can overcome almost any challenge. In fact, we’re often energised by the challenge. What can make a project impossible to approach, however, is a very rigid or complicated relationship with the municipality or third parties that are beyond our control. Nick de Klerk: I think you can work from there, because ultimately we want the same thing. We want the building to be repurposed and brought back into business. Despina Kalapoda: You need to consider many things. How many guest rooms do you need to have? How many guest rooms can you afford to lose to make things functional? Natalia Miyar: One of the biggest obstacles we’ve encountered recently, building on Maria’s point about municipalities and heritage buildings, is when the requirements for environmental upgrades, fire protection and all these other considerations start to eat into the available volume. The number of keys can drop so significantly that the project becomes untenable. Paul Gallacher: Commercial viability is the big one. If it doesn’t stack up, we can’t do anything with it. On a recent project, the more we uncovered of the historic building, the clearer it became that the original vision needed to evolve. By rethinking the approach and allowing the character and constraints of the building to inform the direction, we were able to arrive at a proposition that made much more sense for the building – completely transforming its potential as a hotel. Image credit: Photographer London The conversation continued, digging deeper into understanding the balance between ambition and practicality as a recurring theme in adaptive reuse . A building may have all the architectural appeal in the world, but if the number of rooms, operational requirements or cost of bringing it up to modern standards don’t add up, the project simply won’t work. Sometimes, it was agreed, the answer lies in being prepared to reconsider the original vision. Sophie: Have you ever had to challenge a client’s vision because you could see that their ambitions weren’t quite right for the building? How do you navigate that conversation without losing sight of what they want to achieve? Kim: We had a situation where the owner of a property had a very strong vision for the hotel brand, but the narrative didn’t quite fit. Following conversations with the operator, the positioning evolved into something that was much more appropriate for the property. It was initially a difficult conversation to have with the owner, but it worked out well. Paul: Everyone in our team has a real can-do attitude, and that’s kind of the fun of the job – trying to make something that’s impossible, possible. items.title: Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat  
  Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat • Hotel Designs Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 12, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Miniview: 1898 Porter’s house – an intimate luxury retreat Set discreetly along Ghent’s historic canals, 1898 Porter’s house marks the quiet transformation of a once-modest service building into an intimate hotel shaped by place, memory, and atmosphere… Following the acclaimed success of 1898 The Post, Interior Designer – and The Brit List 2026 Finalist – Geraldine Dohogne has been sought out once again to lead the design of this next chapter – an appointment that reflects the enduring resonance of her emotionally driven, materially honest approach to hospitality design. Image credit: Anthony Van Startum “1898 Porter’s house is for me much more than designing a hotel – I’m immersing guests into a story, not simply creating a space to accommodate them; it’s a sophisticated space that respects the guests needs and builds a world around them.” Geraldine Dohogne Previously responsible for the interiors of 1898 The Post, Geraldine Dohogne returns to a building intrinsically linked to its history. The former Porter’s house of the Hôtel des Postes et des Télégraphes, now 1898 The Post, is reimagined not as a replica of the past, but as a living continuation of it, transformed into a deeply personal retreat that honours its origins while speaking unmistakably to the present. Image credit: Anthony Van Startum “I create emotions, material richness, and a sense of belonging that elevates the hotel into more than a destination but into an experience. Spaces are intimate and personal, playing with subtle layers of history, a rich present and a renewed legacy in the making.” – Geraldine Dohogne Known for a design language defined by authenticity, restraint, and atmosphere rather than trend, Geraldine draws inspiration from Ghent’s working port and the raw character of the Graslei. Her signature use of permanent, tactile materials – wood, leather, marble, and heavy textiles – forms the backbone of the interiors. These elements are chosen for their ability to age and gain character over time, reinforcing a sense of truth and continuity that has become central to her signature style. Image credit: Anthony Van Startum The intimate scale of 1898 Porter’s house allows Geraldine Dohogne’s layered approach to fully unfold. Spaces are proportioned with care, light is treated as a material in its own right, and transitions are gradual – echoing the building’s original role as a place of pause and welcome. A refined yet expressive colour palette, anchored in reds and enriched with undertones of green, blue, and gold, brings depth and warmth without excess, creating interiors that feel immersive, sensual, and quietly sophisticated. With just four rooms and suites, every detail is considered. Custom-designed furniture responds to the building’s historic constraints, integrating desks, minibars, and storage seamlessly within existing architectural elements. Lighting is layered and adaptable, enabling guests to shape their own atmosphere, while views are framed as moments of experience; whether bathing with sight-lines to Ghent’s clock tower or stepping onto a private terrace overlooking the water. Image credit: Anthony Van Startum One of the suites opens onto secluded terraces above the Graslei canal, conceived as extensions of the interiors rather than separate outdoor spaces, whilst the other terrace has a prime view on the clock tower. Naturally shielded by carved stone balustrades, the terraces offer a sense of retreat and calm, functioning as private lounge areas: immersive and discreet, urban yet deeply restful. Rather than emulate the grandeur of large luxury hotels, 1898 Porter’s house continues Dohogne’s long-held belief that true luxury lies in emotion rather than display. Amenities are fully integrated, never ostentatious, supporting a guesthouselike experience that feels personal, grounded, and authentic. It is an approach that made 1898 The Post so enduringly successful – and one that now finds an even more intimate expression here. As a reflection of Dohogne’s evolving practice, 1898 Porter’s house reaffirms her commitment to truth, context, and craftsmanship. With her Belgian design roots, her interiors embrace warmth, colour, and sensual layering. The result is a space that grows richer over time – timeless, emotionally resonant, and once that beckons return visits.   Domes announces three new hotel openings for 2027  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Domes announces three new hotel openings for 2027 • Hotel Designs Domes announces three new hotel openings for 2027 WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 11, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Domes announces three new hotel openings for 2027 Following its acquisition of Casa Collective in April 2026, Domes Resorts has announced three new hotel openings in Greece for 2027. The expansion will see Casa Cook debut in Halkidiki and Santorini, alongside a new Cook’s Club property in Kassandra… The three openings reflect Domes Resorts’ continued expansion following its acquisition of Casa Collective, while building on the individual identities of Casa Cook and Cook’s Club, marking the next phase of development for the lifestyle hospitality brands. Casa Cook Athos will open in northern Greece in summer 2027, reviving a 1959 modernist landmark overlooking a sheltered bay on the lesser-known peninsula near the gateway to Mount Athos. Originally designed by one of Greece’s leading architects, Periklis Sakellarios, and now reimagined by Berlin-based studio Vision Alphabet, the 60-key hotel’s architectural character has been preserved through a sensitive restoration with Casa Cook’s distinctive, understated design, and will open a further 45 rooms its second stage. The hotel will welcome guests aged 12 and over with rooms, suites and a villa, two restaurants with local dishes and wines that reflect paréa (the Greek spirit of togetherness), direct beach access, and a spa with Yoga, breathwork, meditation and sound rituals amongst its wellness programming. The region’s spiritual heritage plays a key role: Mount Olympus, the legendary home of the ancient gods, to the west; Mount Athos with its monastic community history to the east: and in between, Halkidiki with its wooded hills, sheltered bays, fishing villages and clear Aegean waters. Casa Cook Athos itself sits near Ouranoupoli – “City of Heaven”- overlooking a sheltered bay facing Ammouliani and the Drenia islands, and serves as a starting point to explore the destination. Image credit: Cook’s Club Kassandra The launch of Cook’s Club Kassandra marks the next evolution of the brand, introducing its first property on the Greek mainland alongside a new creative direction. Scheduled to open in summer 2027 among the pine-covered hills of Kriopigi on Halkidiki’s western peninsula, this adults-only property resembles a relaxed, private summer house. It centres around the main pool and pool bar area where relaxed, music-filled afternoons transition into livelier evenings. The Boathouse, an open kitchen and restaurant, offers locally sourced dishes, the spa and outdoor gym are accompanied by yoga platform, and the landscaped gardens provide social areas for extended relaxation. Art plays a heightened role with contemporary pieces and large murals displayed throughout the hotel, and a collaboration with Brazilian artist Luciano Cian marks the beginning of a wider series of creative partnerships, from original works and live murals to occasional artist residencies. Casa Cook Santorini will be the third property to open next year, launching in early Q2 2027 in the village of Firostefani with just six traditional cave-style residences, designed to offer a different way to experience the island. Rooted in the island’s traditional whitewashed cave houses with striking Caldera views, the adults-only boutique hotel brings the brand’s design philosophy to a more personal scale, through Concierge’s tailored experiences, the privacy of one’s own residence, and the flexibility to discover the island at one’s own pace for an intimate escape. “The acquisition of Casa Collective represents an important step in our growth strategy, allowing us to expand our lifestyle ecosystem while building on the distinct identities of Casa Cook and Cook’s Club. These three openings in hotels we own showcase how much we believe in the soul and the character of these brands”, said Dr. George P. Spanos, CEO of Domes Resorts and Chairman of Casa Collective. “As Casa Collective grows, we’re building on our deeper understanding of our guests to create meaningful reasons to return, with experiences that respect the individual character of each brand and destination”, states Remo Masala, Founder of Casa Collective and Vision Alphabet. items.summary:

 From woven detail to statement pattern: new Autumn Collections from Newmor

 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: From woven detail to statement pattern: new Autumn Collections from Newmor • Hotel Designs From woven detail to statement pattern: new Autumn Collections from Newmor WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 11, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio From woven detail to statement pattern: new Autumn Collections from Newmor Hot off the press – Newmor introduces three new wallcovering collections for autumn winter 2026, bringing craftsmanship, heritage and quiet luxury into focus… Chambray, Zenith III and Separa – the new 2026 Autumn Collection from Newmor draws on Evergreen, one of the company’s key design trends for the year, exploring a balance of subtle texture, bold pattern and confident colour. Rose Campbell, Head of Design and Marketing, explained the thinking behind the collections, “Our Evergreen trend is rooted in enduring design values. Rich patterns, layered textures and tactile materials come together to create interiors that feel reassuring, familiar and quietly luxurious. Decorative detailing and materiality enhance the unmistakable sense of heritage, while the palette remains grounded and sophisticated with just a touch of the unexpected.” Chambray | Image credit: Newmor Chambray takes its inspiration from its namesake, a traditional linen or cotton fabric first produced in the French town of Cambrai. Newmor has recreated this look by using contrasting prints to build depth within the woven effect, using their cotton emboss to enhance the designs three-dimensional appearance. The result captures the detail and texture of this timeless cloth on a wallcovering surface. Its 12 colourways combine warm, reassuring tones with accents of royal blue, rust and duck egg, offering scope for both tonal interiors and stronger colour combinations. Zenith III Jute | Image credit: Newmor Zenith III brings together four complementary designs, each available in six colourways. Network has a delicately structured open weave, while Supine introduces a subtle horizontal wood plank effect. Brith, named after the Welsh word for speckled, evokes the cosy texture of a woollen blanket. Jute completes the collection with a vertical grasscloth design, combining multiple prints with a detailed emboss. Core neutrals run through the collection, alongside green, pink and mauve accents. The four designs can be used individually or together, introducing changes in texture while maintaining a connection through colour. “With Chambray and Zenith III, much of the interest lies in the finer detail,” says Rose. “Combining print with carefully chosen embosses allows us to create nuanced textures that capture the character of the materials that inspired us, from classic weaves to organic grasscloths. These designs provide a versatile backdrop for a wide variety of commercial interiors.” Image credit: Newmor Newmor has made a considered material choice in both stocked collections: Chambray and Zenith III each contain 20% recycled content, helping to reduce reliance on virgin materials while remaining readily available to customers. Chambray is a 460g Type II nonwoven wallcovering; Zenith III has a 350g scrim/nonwoven construction. Separa brings a bolder dimension to Newmor’s autumn launch. Taking its name from the Samoan word for zebra, the design combines a leather patchwork effect with graphic animal-inspired markings. A fur emboss adds another layer of tactile detail. Separa | Image credit: Newmor The six colourways include classic black and beige, softer tonal combinations, and a new navy and chocolate-plum pairing that reflects an emerging colour direction. “Separa introduces the unexpected element within Evergreen,” Rose adds. “Its pattern has a strong presence, but the colourways give it very different moods. The deeper tones draw out its sophisticated side, while the green feels particularly playful.” Separa is a stocked digital design printed on a 460g Type II nonwoven base. Newmor Wallcoverings is one of our Recommended Suppliers and regularly features in our Supplier News section of the website. If you are interested in becoming one of our Recommended Suppliers, please email Katy Phillips.   Mar by O’Two Hotels to open on Cape Town’s Mouille Point  
 Sienna Shipton .
items.text: Mar by O’Two Hotels to Open in Mouille Point, Cape Town Mar by O’Two Hotels to open on Cape Town’s Mouille Point WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 11, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Mar by O’Two Hotels to open on Cape Town’s Mouille Point Opening in March 2027, Mar joins Terra on the Platinum Mile as O’Two Hotels becomes a dual-concept group, with 68 residential-style rooms, a rooftop pool and a dedicated spa floor to follow… O’Two Hotels is set to open Mar, a luxury oceanfront hotel on the Mouille Point coast, in March 2027. The Cape Town boutique group is evolving into a dual-concept brand, with Mar sitting alongside the existing lifestyle-led Terra to offer two distinct ways of experiencing the city from a single address on the Platinum Mile. The hotels occupy a ribbon of Atlantic oceanfront between the sea and a protected urban green belt, with views taking in Table Mountain, Signal Hill, Lion’s Head and the ocean horizon. The group takes its identity from this meeting of sea and land, which is expressed in Mar and Terra, each with its own character and philosophy. Image credit: O’Two Hotels Mar is conceived as a refined oceanfront retreat for guests who value space, privacy and a personalised approach to luxury. Open layouts, ocean light and uninterrupted Atlantic views shape the interiors, while amenities include a rooftop pool, a heated open-air deck and destination dining. The hotel has 68 residential-style guest rooms, 28 of them spacious suites. Each has a private balcony, a workstation and a walk-in rain shower stocked with Voya amenities. Interconnecting configurations suit families and groups while keeping each suite private. “Mar represents a defining moment for O’Two Hotels and a natural evolution of our vision,” says Riaan Sinclair Drever, Managing Director of O’Two Hotels. “As we grow, our commitment remains unchanged: to deliver exceptional hospitality through genuine service, thoughtful design and meaningful guest experiences.” Image credit: O’Two Hotels Metamorph Spa and Wellness joins Mar in October 2027, occupying its own dedicated floor on the eighth level. Conceived as a place to slow down, it offers ocean views and bespoke full-body journeys tailored to individual wellbeing needs. Facilities include a sauna, hammam, ice plunge pool and mineral pool. Advanced facials and aesthetic clinic treatments are delivered by expert aesthetic doctors and visiting practitioners, using local and international organic products. A state-of-the-art gym and wellness studio completes the offering, with classes spanning sound healing, Pilates, yoga, grounding and meditation. Until the spa opens, Mar guests have full access to the O’Two Spa and fitness centre at Terra. Where Mar invites stillness, Terra invites movement. The group’s existing hotel draws inspiration from the mountains, the rugged beauty of the Karoo and South Africa’s biodiversity. Its 33 rooms and suites combine contemporary interiors with social spaces, and suit travellers who want to tune into the pulse of the city. Guests can move between exploring Cape Town and poolside downtime, with access to the rooftop pool, O’Two Spa and fitness centre. Image credit: O’Two Hotels Two celebrated South African restaurant concepts, Le Parc and Kolonaki, open on Mouille Point’s boulevard in December 2026, ahead of Mar. Le Parc brings the joie de vivre of Paris to the seafront. Part food emporium, it draws on the French capital’s cafés, patisseries and markets. Guests can browse sweet treats and freshly baked bread at the bakery, shop for artisanal products or settle in for a leisurely lunch of classic French cooking with a contemporary twist. Colourful interiors, candy-striped details and floral displays inspired by French flower markets complete the picture. Kolonaki channels Greek hospitality and meze culture. Led by Chef Vassilios Holiasmenos, it welcomes every guest like family, with a menu built around sharing. The small plates, which range from homemade dips to tempura aubergine, are designed to encourage diners to linger. Image credit: O’Two Hotels More relaxed alfresco dining is available at the pool decks, where dishes from Kolonaki can be enjoyed beside The Terrace or with panoramic views at The Rooftop. Papillon, a laid-back lounge defined by a crystal butterfly chandelier and rich green interiors, serves coffee by day and expertly crafted cocktails by night. Mouille Point is a relaxed, compact and walkable residential neighbourhood, known for its seafront promenade busy with runners and cyclists, independent cafés, historic lighthouse and memorable sunsets. It is minutes from the V&A Waterfront, the city centre and Cape Town Stadium, and a short drive from Table Mountain, Camps Bay and Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, pairing access to the city’s cultural and culinary scene with the calm of a seaside neighbourhood. items.text: Delano London to open early 2027 • Hotel Designs Delano London to open early 2027 WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 10, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Delano London to open early 2027 Overlooking Kensington Gardens and Hyde Park, among the grand Victorian buildings and embassies of one of London’s most distinguished neighbourhoods, Delano London marks a new chapter for the celebrated hotel brand, opening early 2027… Drawing on a legacy that spans Miami, Dubai and Paris, the 67 room and suite hotel brings Delano’s distinctive sensibility for magnetic nightlife, story-led dining and innovative wellness to the capital. Across five floors, more than half of the rooms will be suites, with 14 offering prime views across Hyde Park. Designed by Archer Humphryes Architects , Delano London brings the spirit of Delano Miami Beach into a distinctly West London setting. Residential interiors and subtly theatrical details create an atmosphere of discovery. Image credit: Delano London / Ennismore At the heart of the hotel’s dining experience is Lana Lusa, designed by Pirajean Lees and brought to London for the first time by internationally acclaimed hospitality group Paris Society. Created by founder Jessica Viveiro Kassim, the concept celebrates the warmth and conviviality of Mediterranean hospitality. Within the hotel sits a cocktail destination Rose Bar which brings Delano’s iconic after-dark spirit to the city, reimagining the glamour of its legendary Miami Beach counterpart. Within the space, the Rose Bar Lounge and the Zodiac Room offer more intimate settings for late-night revelry. The Source by Delano will offer a fresh approach to wellness, centred around restorative and rejuvenating movement and longevity. Contrast therapy, treatment spaces and state-of-the-art facilities will sit alongside a changing roster of leading practitioners, residencies and collaborations with some of the world’s most exciting names in wellness. Image credit: Delano London / Ennismore London-based art consultancy Cramer & Bell have curated an original collection, celebrating British art alongside established international artists. Highlights include South African artist Kimathi Mafafo,and London-based artists Isaac Andrews, Hormazd Narielwalla, and Gergei Erdei. Completing the experience, Delano Members Club brings together a global community of creative, accomplished and curious minds. Members will have access to a programme of experiences, partnerships and privileges extending beyond the hotel, both locally and internationally. ‘Delano Beyond’, a global programme, will provide members with bespoke travel experiences. “Delano has always been about creating a feeling’’ commented Ben Pundole, Chief Brand Officer for Delano Hotels, ‘’Bringing the brand to London feels particularly special because this is my home city with such a rich and varied cultural history. Delano London will be a space for discovery, somewhere you might strike up a conversation at Rose Bar with someone you’d never ordinarily meet, encounter a work by an emerging artist, or simply settle into an atmosphere that transports you beyond the bustle of the city outside. It’s a place for those who look for unique experiences.” Main image credit: Delano London / Ennismore You might also like Ennismore signs Delano Puglia News / 05.10.2026 The Hoxton set to make its Middle East debut in Dubai News / 11.09.2026 Gleneagles unveils its most glamorous residence yet Hotel Design / 07.09.2026 SPACE: the latest issue In video Latest articles At water level: inside Magma’s Sauna Garden 16.11.2026 In conversation with: Youssef Benabbès Tâarji, AKAN 16.11.2026 Healing by design: inside ŪRJĀ, the Maldives’ new naturopathy island 13.11.2026 Hotel review: El Fenn – cool, calm and colourful in Marrakech 13.11.2026 Roundtable: Layer by Layer: historic buildings as modern hotels 12.11.2026 Receive our newsletter here Recommended suppliers Latest from the DESIGN POD Episode 50: Grant Woodrow – into the Wilderness 03.06.2025 Episode 49: Fettle, the transatlantic design studio with Andy Goodwin and Tom Parker 14.03.2025 Episode 48: Redesigning Historic Buildings with Tom Thorogood 10.01.2025 Episode 47: Form and Function with Nick Hickson 20.12.2024 Episode 46: 40 Years in the Making – David Collins Studio with Lewis Taylor 22.11.2024 Recommended suppliers Upcoming events The Brit List Awards 5th November, 2026 Hotel Summit 22nd April, 2027 This website uses cookies to improve your experience.
