items.title: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques
items.summary:
At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla… 
 The post  Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques — Resy | Right This Way Cotoletta 4.7 · Italian · $ Miami Book Now Published: Nov. 9, 2026 At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla Milanese. No substitutions. No alternatives. Just a golden, pan-fried veal cutlet — and a bet that it’s all you’ll need. Until recently, making a reservation required a phone call, which only deepened the sense that this place operates on its own terms. (The good news: You can now reserve a table on Resy.) The concept debuted in Coconut Grove in the fall of 2024 and comes from 84 Magic Hospitality, a restaurant group known for a growing collection of Miami restaurants with minimalist menus ( San Lorenzo , San Marco , and the lasagna pop-up, Si Papa 3190 , are the others). Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Still, the story behind the concept stretches back further than its Miami address might suggest. Cotoletta is the creation of partners Ignacio Lopez Mancisidor and Mattia Cicognani, and former co-founder Andrea Fraquelli — who share a background in hospitality and a frustration with how transactional the industry had become. From the start, their goal at Cotoletta has been to make things simple for guests and allow them to focus on what really matters: great food and genuine connection. “Across the globe, many of the best restaurants do one item and they do it to absolute perfection,” co-founder Mattia Cicognani says. “We drew inspiration from the Italian essence of committing to one hero dish and prioritizing ingredients of the highest quality.” “Only serving one dish was a risk,” Cicognani acknowledges, “but the popularity and love for the concept has proven that it really works. Our customers learned that they love what we do and that is why they continue to come back.” Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Head chef Davide Rosselli shared the process that delivers a consistent, classic cotoletta every time. Premium veal is hand-trimmed, gently pounded to its thin-yet-tender texture, coated in fresh egg and breadcrumbs, and fried in clarified butter until it emerges with a crisp, even, golden crust. Each cutlet weighs in at roughly 20 ounces, made to be shared between two people. The result is a traditional veal Milanese that is a signature of Northern Italian craftsmanship. Everything else on the table exists to support that centerpiece. “While the process sounds simple, it’s backed by decades of Italian tradition and time-honored techniques passed down by chefs across generations,” Rosselli says. For $90, two diners share the full prix-fixe experience: two antipasti courses of bruschetta and truffle arancino to start, followed by the veal cutlet, and two sides (the only real choice you have to make here). Dessert (tiramisu or a flourless chocolate cake) can be added on for $14. “Each appetizer sets the tone for a true Italian experience, while the sides are thoughtfully chosen to complement the veal without overpowering it.” Rosselli says. “Lighter elements like crisp salads and simple pasta dishes help balance the richness of the veal, creating a well-rounded meal.” Those side options include pasta al pomodoro, zucchine fritte, insalata di rucola, or patatine fritte. Rosselli’s personal picks: the pasta in just the right portion to leave you wanting more of the main event, and the zucchine fritte offering a warm, light bite that balances out the richness of the veal. (Wondering what happens if you bring a third wheel or want to dine solo? Odd-numbered parties can add on an individual portion of bruschetta, arancino, a smaller veal cutlet, and one side for $55.) Guests return because the menu never changes, and neither does the reason to go back. “They know exactly what they are getting every single time,” Cicognani says. Cotoletta is open weekdays from 5:30 to 10 p.m. and until 10:30 p.m. on Friday. On weekends, it opens at 12:30 p.m. until 10:30 p.m. on Saturday and 9 p.m. on Sunday. Lyssa Goldberg is a Miami-based freelance writer and content strategist. She loves telling stories about food, wellness and travel, and you can find her byline in Parade, American Way, Mashable, Miami New Times, Time Out and more. Follow her on Instagram and Twitter . Follow Resy , too. items.text: The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 As people who love restaurants, we know that when it comes to picking a spot for dinner, it’s much more than about just the food. The vibe is just as important, and music is a key player in creating it. Sometimes, the best soundtrack is the one you don’t notice, but the places on this list aren’t for those kinds of nights. These playlists are hyper specific, the sound systems are top of the line, and often they have some of the best vinyl collections in the country, and a guest DJs on weekends who comes in to spin them. These are places you go to for the music, but where us restaurant lovers won’t need to suffer because the snacks that can often lead to full meals are far more interesting than a bag of stale potato chips. You’ll be able to listen to some Japanese jazz deep cuts over an omakase, or eclectic world beats over some of the city’s silkiest hummus — with playlists and menus like these, you might not need to make it to your second destination for the night. And if you’re looking for spots with live music, we’ve got you covered here . City Photo courtesy of 56709 What was once 929, an audio haven for Canto pop, is now a moody, atmospheric spot for Japanese city pop, from the same team. You’ll also find plenty of records that include J-pop from the 90s and 2000s, plus Japanese R&B. And the theme isn’t strictly limited to the music, either. Cocktails are named after Japanese pop stars (Anri, Momoko, Ryuichi) and anime (Agumon, Usagi), and food is a fusion of Japanese and Taiwanese flavors: Think radish cakes with XO sauce, braised pork over rice, and mala-seasoned French fries. Book Now Birds map West Village Whether you’re partial to live music or listening bar vibes, Birds has you covered. On weeknights they spin selections from their enormous vinyl collection, and on weekends they host live musicians in a variety of styles like ska, jazz, and Afrobeats. Know that on Fridays and Saturdays there’s a $30 cover charge, but it’s a small price to pay for the incredible night of music that you’re in for. Book Now Boro Brine map Williamsburg The bar. Photo by Ben Hon, courtesy of Boro Brine There are two concepts at this Williamsburg restaurant, an intimate 22-seat omakase counter and a Japanese-inspired cocktail bar. Audiophiles will be satisfied at either, as music runs throughout and the sound system is top notch. The chef’s tasting consists of an ever-changing menu of multiple courses for $98 a person, whereas the bar has an à la carte menu that features inventive cocktails and bites like a chef’s take on a filet-o-fish and octopus with saag paneer. With velvet banquets and a dimly lit interior, it’s also a perfect date night spot. Book Now ALL BLUES map Tribeca Photo courtesy of All Blues Don’t be surprised if you’re asked to keep quiet at this Tribeca listening room. It’s all about the music here, so much so to that conversation is discouraged. All Blues comes from owner Yuji Fukushima, who based the concept on the places he frequented back growing up in Tokyo. He’s invested in top-tier audio equipment and carefully selects the music each evening, which can range from funk to Dizzy Gillespie. Enjoy Japanese snacks like tempura sweet potatoes and gyoza, alongside a fine whiskey or sake while you take in the sounds. Book Now Record Room map Long Island City Photo courtesy of Record Room This Long Island City bar might be a little hard to find at first, but that’s the idea. Behind a hidden door, you’ll be transported to a music filled living room of sorts, filled with comfy couches and soft lighting. All the music here is played off vinyl and there might be occasional dancing. The drinks lean classic, with riffs on espresso martinis

items.text: 29 New York Bars and Restaurants with Excellent Zero-Proof Cocktails — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 Somewhere around a decade ago the dreaded term “mocktail” first started to surface on menus, referring to drinks meant to offer the cocktail experience, but none of the “buzz.” At the time, unlike their alcoholic counterparts, most of these drinks were overly sweet mixes of juice and housemade sodas with elaborate garnishes. Now, however, there’s been a shift in drinking culture: Dry January, anyone? In other words, we’re drinking less, or thinking about having that second or third drink more, and beverage directors have taken note. Today’s mocktails are now as considered and thoughtfully developed as those made full-strength. Many of them also feature the new wave of non-alcoholic spirits, like Seedlip, Lyre’s, Little Saints, Amass Riverine, and Ghia. So, whether you’re abstaining from alcohol, are taking a night off, or just want to stay and linger at the bar after your glass has run dry, here are some of the best places in the city to find zero-proof cocktails. Newly added: Bar Americano, Lord’s, Overstory, and The Up & Up. on their all-day menu are, well, soft. The Golden Hour , with grape, elderflower, pink peppercorn shrub, and alcohol-free Champagne, or the Pear Pressure with prickly pear, agave, and alcohol-free Tequila, are both good choices. Keep an eye out on the menu for the function of each drink, which ranges from focus to “vibey.” Plus, there’s a celebrity at the helm – fans of Bravo’s Summer House might see a familiar face. Read all about Soft Bar here . Book Now Golden Ratio map Clinton Hill What can’t this team do? Golden Ratio comes from the masterminds behind Cafe Mado and Place des Fêtes , serving up cocktails and mocktails to the Clinton Hill crowd. Nearly all of the cocktails here have a nonalcoholic counterpart, and everything is fiercely flavor-driven and seasonal. Past drinks have included interpretations of purple shiso , apple , and toothache tree , and the team is working towards being zero-waste, so you can have your drink and eat it, too. Book Now Lord's map NoHo This beloved purveyor of British fare may not be the first thing that comes to mind when you think of nonalcoholic beverages, but their list (which they title “Teetotaling”) is one of our favorites. Go for a Blood Orange Spritz , a sour made with Ghia, or a S affron White Negroni — all totally alcohol free, of course. Any of them pairs perfectly with a good lamb Scotch egg, too. Book Now Sofreh map Prospect Heights There’s not a lot we’d say no to at Sofreh. While yes, their list of cocktails is excellent, the real pearl here has to be the selection of sharbats , a Persian cooler that comes in flavors like mint and cucumber, sour cherry, and lemon and saffron. If those aren’t doing it for you, there’s also the Persian black tea and a mint and rose petal yogurt drink. No matter what’s in your glass, make sure an order of herb meatballs and saffron rice are on your table. Book Now The Up & Up map Greenwich Village This subterranean cocktail den and ideal date night spot in Greenwich Village has an extensive list of drinks that also includes five excellent nonalcoholic takes on some of their classics. This includes a zero-proof spin of Hold, Please , a watermelon shrub that draws inspiration from New York’s sliced fruit vendors who often sell servings of watermelon spears topped with Tajín. There’s also an N/A version of Zuzu’s Petals , named for the classic film, “It’s a Wonderful Life,” that’s made with ginger, habanero, rose water, lime juice, and demerara. Book Now Spygold map Hudson Yards Greywind’s (also on this list) sister and downstairs neighbor, the fire-lit Spygold, has an equally lovely list of non-alcoholic options for you to peruse. Past favorites have included the Tomato, Tomahto with nonalcoholic gin and tomato-basil soda, or the Cucumber Highball with alcohol-free Tequila and cucumber soda. items.title: Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core
items.summary: The 119-mile inn-to-inn hiking route has reconnected mountain villages in Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, once splintered by war—and welcomed the world onto their doorstep.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania . Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away. I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves. The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo , and Montenegro . Amber Dunlap/@nomapsamber Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats. Amber Dunlap/@nomapsamber It’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in. This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo , and Montenegro , through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration. The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle. Amber Dunlap/@nomapsamber By those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest. Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel company Zbulo , which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He says the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the issue. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October. After breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol. Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude. Amber Dunlap/@nomapsamber All except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain. At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century. Ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it. “This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.” Having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago

items.title: What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out
items.summary: Writer Bridget Knowles seeks out the Austrian philosophy behind Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort in Austria’s Großarl Valley that encourages guests to get in the buff.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof , an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großar l Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened. In Austria , being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate. Großar l Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria. Originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by big name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany ’s neighbor, Austria. Language, of course, falls short when attempting to describe what Lebensgefühl means in practice; this complete awareness of being is a physicality, an emotion, a lifestyle, and a philosophy all rolled into one. It can’t be described, only felt (ah!). It’s the pleasure of simply existing. Leben (life), Gefühl (feeling). It’s an experience I wanted to understand firsthand. So when I found myself in Munich, less than a two-hour train ride from Hotel Nesslerhof, with a lifelong friend oblivious to my schemes, I decided it was time to get to the bottom of it. The root of Lebensgefühl is being entirely present in a moment: a conscious effort to slow down, gauge your own energy in the here and now, and choose the way you want to live your life accordingly. While the Austrian National Tourist Board uses the concept of Lebensgefühl as a marketing language, the feeling itself is real–and you can cultivate it anywhere. Admittedly, though—hand of accountability raised—it’s a whole lot easier when you’re surrounded by the postcard-perfect Austrian Alps. Reaching this state of awareness requires an analog attention span and total presence. This is exactly what is demanded of you at Hotel Nesslerhof, which has dubbed itself the “natural happiness hotel.” The sprawling, sun-warmed property is an emerald-colored garden punctured by buttery blonde oak 1643 Austrian longhouse architecture. Here, the world is calm. Quiet. I arrive burned out, my attention scattered across screens and obligations. Stepping into a place fully immersed in nature with nothing expected of me, is jarring. It's been a while since I've consumed life this way. We’re conditioned to scroll, desire, save, project, and imagine, rather than to simply be—even to just be for a little bit. Finding the answer started with carving out time and space, and letting go of everything I thought presence was supposed to look like. Next thing, I was naked in Austria with 40 strangers wondering the same thing. Natural swimming pond for post-sauna plunges in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older. Courtesy Nesslerhof The saunas The hotel’s dedicated wellness area features five co-ed clothing-optional saunas (plus an additional private sauna in select suites), a salt steam bath, infrared loungers, and expansive natural swimming pools. To practice, or fully embody, Lebensgefühl successfully, you must be aware of your environment. At Nesslerhof, the alpine nature allows your body to break away from any externally imposed schedules and return back to your natural circadian rhythm, where an omniscient digital third person doesn't determine your flow; you do. A Swiss pine sauna in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older. As a lifelong advocate for a good time, I mustered some gumption to join one of the daily themed sauna “infusions.” During these sessions, a sauna master leads thematic experiences using natural, regional botanicals like thyme, sage, Swiss stone pine, and eucalyptus. It’s held in the adults-only sauna event room, a space large enough to accommodate nearly 50 people. I walk in—towel on—and it occurs to me I’m the one making it weird here. There’s a lot I can swallow in life, but one thing I certainly will not do is be the person making things weird in a room. So, I lose the towel, join the crowd, and, in a state of mild panic, take a seat on the floor. Now, retrospectively speaking, I couldn’t grasp how all my choices in life had led me to this single, very conscious state of nudity in front of 40 Austrian strangers. There I was—sitting on the floor, completely floored. Which actually made things weirder, because I was later told you aren’t supposed to sit on the floor. Enter the sauna master. Also nude. A sauna master is like a spiritual guide to a proper schvitz, and the infusions at Nesslerhof are next level material. At pivotal moments, I’m watching him execute rainbow ice acrobatics, teasing large, colorful chunks of ice around the room in a giant spoon before launching them onto the glowing-hot stones. Steam is sizzling everywhere as thick aromatics sweep across the room. Hotel Nesslerhof's outdoor saltwater pool (with indoor access) surrounded by the Großarl Valley. And it’s hot . To make matters worse for myself—still on the floor—we’re given a natural body scrub to apply. So, whatever, sure: I start scrubbing amidst the rainbow ice, dense botanical air, and naked strangers unabashedly sprawled across the room in their entirety. I begin to gain consciousness of the palpable sense of self-assurance emanating from everyone as they laughed and chatted heart-to-heart. They were all having…fun. Slowly, decidedly, I reach a state of compos mentis: the only thing mortifying about this experience is my belief that this is a mort

items.summary: From thermal baths powered by hot springs to top-level tanks with skyline views, these indoor pools are sure to stun.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story It’s hard to nail an indoor pool —they can very easily veer into athletic club territory, where the smell of chlorine is inescapable, and every splash seems to elicit an unwanted echo. Outdoor pools, with their trompe l’oeil effects and decadent sun loungers, often get most of the credit, but some of their indoor counterparts can pull off even better architectural shows. From thermal baths powered by hot springs to top-level tanks with skyline views, the indoor pools on this list are nothing short of spectacular—not to mention, they can be enjoyed year-round, so you won’t miss out when it rains in New York or Paris. Far from your YMCA, these pools have design details you’ll swoon over: skylights, floor-to-ceiling windows, vaulted ceilings, mosaic tiling, and more. Yes, these hotels are worth booking for the awe-inspiring swims alone. Read on for the best indoor pools at hotels around the world, spanning Mexico to Vietnam . items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Family vacations come in all shapes and sizes, but sometimes, it’s all about the kids. That’s when places like Great Wolf Lodge come in clutch. Between the indoor water parks, arcades, and arts and crafts, they’re designed for keeping bundles of energy entertained…both kids and kids at heart. I’ve been to a Great Wolf Lodge once (in LaGrange, just outside of Atlanta) and had a ball going down those water slides and playing arcade games, even as a kid-free twenty-something. Points are not earned on any alcohol purchases, taxes, gratuities, fees, or on-site purchases not charged to the suite. items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Marriott Coupon Codes You never forget your first dolphin encounter—and for many kids across the country, that often happens at SeaWorld. The beloved oceanarium puts the “amusement” in amusement parks: orcas leaping in the air, floorless rollercoasters named after sea monsters, and even aquarium sleepovers. With parks in Orlando, San Diego, San Antonio, and Abu Dhabi, SeaWorld’s aquatic allure has no bounds. SeaWorld is a top choice when it comes to taking the family out for some educational fun. Established in 1964 by four UCLA graduates, SeaWorld began in San Diego with 22 acres, six attractions, and a handful of sea lions and dolphins (beloved orca whale Shamu arrived at the party a year later). In the early 2000s, the parks expanded with thrill rides and rollercoasters, as well as Discovery Cove, allowing visitors to interact with marine animals like bottlenose dolphins. Over the course of its history, SeaWorld has rescued over 40,000 animals and, through the SeaWorld and Busch Gardens Conservation Fund , donated over $19 million to global projects, from restoring coral reefs to preventing coastal erosion. If you want your little ones to have a whale of a time, here are the best SeaWorld Parks promo codes, discounts, and deals. Save up to 60% off tickets during the Black Friday presale Take advantage of SeaWorld's Black Friday discounts. Save up to 60% on tickets, fun cards, and passes. Save over 50% on a single-day ticket to SeaWorld San Diego ($65 instead of $130) and enjoy increased flexibility if you visit before March 31, 2027. Combine it with the All-Day Dining option for $40, and you won't have to worry about buying meals. You can also save 40% on a 2027 Fun Card and take advantage of unlimited free visits to SeaWorld San Diego now through 2027 ($78 from $130). Active-duty military personnel can get free admission SeaWorld expresses its gratitude for the service of military members through the Waves of Honor program, which grants any US active-duty military, activated or drilling reservist, or National Guardsman one complimentary admission per year, and tickets for as many as three direct dependents. Military personnel can also enjoy a 50% off discount on up to six SeaWorld Orlando single-day tickets, plus a Silver Annual Pass at SeaWorld Orlando (unlimited admission with no blockout dates for 12 months) for $161 instead of $279. Those who can take advantage of this offer will need to verify their identity via ID.Me . Veterans can save 50% on SeaWorld tickets For military personnel who have completed their service, SeaWorld is offering 50% off single-day tickets at SeaWorld Orlando, plus the same Silver Annual Pass discount that active-duty military members get to enjoy. To take advantage of this offer, verify with ID.Me . Kids five and under can enjoy free preschool passes If you’ve got a preschooler , give them the gift of maximum aquarium time. At SeaWorld San Antonio, kids under the age of five can enjoy free, unlimited admission to SeaWorld until January 2027, plus unlimited visits to Aquatica for only $39—just be sure to register before the offer expires on May 30. Preschool Cards are limited to Texas residents only. Teachers can gain free access with the SeaWorld Florida Teacher Card Because SeaWorld is dedicated to research and education, the theme park offers certified K–12 teachers in Florida free admission. The SeaWorld Florida Teacher Card is valid for unlimited admission to SeaWorld Orlando through September 2, 2027. All teachers have to do is pre-register on ID.Me with a Department of Education (DOE) number. Plus, Florida Teacher Card holders have the option to add Aquatica Orlando for only $49.99. Find deals on annual passes for SeaWorld discounts in 2026 If you find yourself visiting the dolphins often, consider investing in an annual pass for the lowest cost per visit. Annual passes often include perks like free guest tickets and discounts on food and merchandise. During the sale , prices for passes are reduced for new members: Save up to 15% on the Bronze Pass, 20% on Silver, 25% on Gold, and 30% on Platinum. Using a SeaWorld Parks promo code annual pass deal can pay for itself in just two visits. Check if the code is park-specific (for example, a SeaWorld Orlando promo code may not work for San Diego). And finally, ensure you are not trying to stack, let’s say, an AAA discount with a military offer, as most SeaWorld discounts cannot be combined. items.text: North America Chevron United States Chevron Arizona Chevron Grand Canyon Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby. Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to. Here are my favorite Grand Canyon hotels, glamping sites, vacation rentals, and cabins for a memorable stay in and around this utterly striking national park. items.title: These 9 Hotels for Broadway Lovers Put You in the Heart of NYC’s Theater District
items.summary: From themed suites and ticket access to hotels with major theater lore, here's where to stay on a Broadway-centric trip.
items.text: North America Chevron United States Chevron New York Chevron New York Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story As a Californian who discovered the wonderful world of Broadway by borrowing CDs from my local library, it was only fitting that the first trip I ever planned by myself was to New York City—and the entire itinerary revolved around collecting Playbills. Now, after living in the area for more than two decades, I’m that unlikely New Yorker who still claims Times Square as her favorite and most-frequented neighborhood. I just love the Theater District—where else can you find 41 venues featuring the world's best live theater all within a single mile? In this age of event tourism, Broadway has remained a constant. And seeing a show is about more than just the storyline of a play or the numbers in a musical—it’s an experience that you’re a part of. Over my 20 years as an entertainment editor and journalist, I’ve interviewed numerous Broadway stars, and they always say they feed off of, and are fueled by, audience reactions. You’re not just a passive viewer; your presence drives the show. It's something special to take part in. If you've got a Broadway trip in your future, chances are you're going to need a hotel that will help you maximize your experience. The list below features properties with themed suites, theater lore, and locations just steps from the Great White Way. Read on for the best places to stay in NYC for a show-stopping Broadway getaway. items.title: Bar Le Trente
items.summary: La entrada  Bar Le Trente  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Bar Le Trente — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Design , Food Bar Le Trente The Wild Child of Pigalle Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Tanguy Sergheraert Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share Following Hotel Massé , siblings Corto and Eole Peyron have opened Le Trente. Located next to the hotel, this bar occupies an iconic former loft in Pigalle, transforming it into a place for encounters with both neighbourhood locals and travellers. Like Massé, it draws on the family motto, “make a friend a day”, though its world is slightly different. “Le Trente is a bit like Hotel Massé’s more unruly younger brother. They belong to the same family, but they don’t quite have the same character”, explains Eole. At Massé, calm and intimacy prevail. Step through the doors of Le Trente, however, and the energy shifts: drinks, food , friends and DJs spinning vinyl from Thursday onwards. Close While touches of velvet, wood and beige give the hotel its soft, inviting aesthetic, Le Trente feels sexier and bolder: leather, mirrors and very low lighting in the evening. Once again, Olivier Guyot and studio Gasparetto Parenti worked with the Peyron family to rethink the space and bring Le Trente to life. Outside, the lettering and green marble frontage mark the entrance to this singular place. Inside, a raw, conceptual universe takes shape: a large vintage wooden bar, red-painted floors, high and low seating, small tables and even an outdoor alcove. Close As at Massé, every object has been sourced second-hand or custom-made. “We really didn’t want everything to feel new or perfectly matched”, Eole notes. “There are things we found, contemporary artworks, pieces made specifically for the space and objects and memories from our family”. This is precisely what creates a space that feels both artistic and homely: the walls are covered with personal photographs featuring familiar faces, many of them tracing the expeditions of their father, Stéphane Peyron. Close “Our father has spent his life travelling and meeting people in some of the most remote parts of the world”, Eole comments. “He taught us that it’s the people you meet who make the journey and the memories”. This philosophy, central to both Corto and Eole, runs through Le Trente and is what prompted them to open a bar alongside the hotel. “At Le Trente, Massé guests mix with neighbours and Parisians. You can come for dinner, have a drink, celebrate a birthday, hold an exhibition or a book signing”. Close This same understanding of connections with people from all walks of life extends to their team. Some were friends before the project was born; others have become friends along the way: “The Massé and Le Trente teams are young and very close-knit. It wasn’t something we planned – it just happened naturally”. Close Gabrielle, a young neighbourhood sommelier who knocked on the door during the renovation, curates a minimalist selection of natural wines from France and beyond. Louis, a neighbour of Le Trente and a music enthusiast, is in charge of the music programme. Discovered at listening sessions, on the radio or in the city’s record shops, Le Trente’s DJs share one passion: vinyl. Ambient, house, jazz, downtempo or electro. Corto and his childhood friend Cyril teamed up with Félix to imagine Le Trente’s menu, built around a simple question: what do we want to eat in a bar? The answers became the menu: simple but really good dishes, designed for sharing. Close The menu changes weekly and follows the seasons, so regulars can keep coming back without tiring of the same dishes. The music rotates in a similar way: “We tend to favour artists from the local scene, whether emerging or already established, and we give them a lot of freedom”. Each artist brings their own records, generating a mood that is personal yet lively. “Le Trente never has exactly the same soundtrack two nights in a row, and that’s exactly how we like it”. Close Upstairs, you walk into a huge glass-roofed room: “You can almost feel as though you’re in a New York loft, until you look outside and see the Haussmann façades – you see Paris”. A contrast that sums up the place perfectly. Family, vintage, modernity and intention coexist naturally at Le Trente. The room has an immediate depth and character, and nothing feels forced: instinctively, you feel at home, whether it’s your first visit or you’re a regular. items.title: Badi Restaurant
items.summary: La entrada  Badi Restaurant  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Badi Restaurant — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design , Food Badi Restaurant A Layered Sense of Taste Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Adrien Maurice & Benjamin Baltus Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share For Victoria Merret and Maxime Bourdigal, Badi embraces everything: their job, their interests, their tastes, their values, and their personality. In other words, Badi embodies the couple’s vision. Every sphere comes together under the same sensibility: a pursuit of balance between beauty, precision, and flavour. At Badi, located in Saint-Gilles (Brussels), design , materials, and cuisine interact seamlessly. Initially, the idea sparked for a cider bar: “We kept saying to ourselves: ‘We’d love to go to a wine bar that serves a hundred different ciders,’ so we decided to create it.” As a product that hits close to home with their Breton roots, it seemed like an effortless path to take. Close Nevertheless, three years after opening, Badi has now established itself as a fully-fledged restaurant. “We rediscovered ourselves through the world of natural wine,” and the evolution came instinctively. A place where raw products and ingredients are at the centre of everything, and that is guided by honesty, quality and craftsmanship. The menu and the space complement each other, sculpting an experience that is both curated yet welcoming. In the kitchen, Maxime, who has worked for Bertrand Larcher in Paris and Japan, as well as Ötap in Brussels, collaborates with Paul-Antoine Bertin (Rebel, Grain, Raki, Ötap…) to develop product-centred menus. For the interior, the couple worked with Nelly Smets. Close “We immediately connected through a shared vision regarding materials and influences, but the challenge was then to make all the elements work together harmoniously,” they comment. Inspired by Nordic and Japanese style, raw elements were non-negotiable. Wood, natural stone, steel, textured walls… They all come together around the protagonist of the show. Close A large central travertine counter dominates the space, defining a cohesive and immersive experience. And that was the intention from the beginning: “The central counter encourages interaction with our guests because everyone is seated at the same height, forming a closeness.” The environment becomes convivial, light, easygoing, and authentic. “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” “The design of the space is much more connected to the food and drinks selection than people might think.” Built by craftsmen with honest materials, this philosophy equally translates to the curation of the menu: “It’s just as we do when selecting our natural ciders, wines, and ingredients for the kitchen.” Constantly adapting to the seasons, every menu balances freshness, indulgence, comfort, and elegance, while keeping everything approachable and never overly complex. Close This same ethos translates to Victoria and Maxime’s home: “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” Separating work and private life, the apartment was also driven by the desire to work with raw resources, with wood playing a very important role, but this time in a more personal way. Close “For the restaurant, we tried to develop the most timeless design possible so it could age beautifully over the years. For the apartment, however, we allowed ourselves to make stronger choices to build something with a more distinctive identity.” Altogether, with the help of Nelly Smets and, for their home, her daughter Iolie Coufo. Close In both spaces, the couple is present in many ways. “We constantly dig into memories, experiences, and travels to shape our inspirations; a mix of different influences and emotions we’ve collected over the years, brought together in a way that feels genuinely ours.” For Victoria and Maxime, interior design is about much more than conceiving beautiful places; it’s about shaping spaces where people come to create meaningful moments. items.title: Jaç HiFI Café
items.summary: La entrada  Jaç HiFI Café  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Jaç HiFI Café — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design Jaç HiFI Café A 21st century temple of sound Photographed by Salva López Written by Openhouse Studio Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share A new café has taken over Avinguda Diagonal 335, in the heart of Barcelona: JAÇ HiFi Café. Designed by Isern Serra Studio , the space opened in July 2025 with not one, but two missions: to invite guests to drink coffee and to listen. In fact, its name carries multiple meanings: a nod to jazz music itself, a reference to Japan’s jazz kissa and in Catalan, the word “jaç,” which means to recline, rest, and let go. But, what were jazz kissa ? Characterized by compact and dimly lit venues, these spaces were intimate listening bars that flourished from the 1950s onwards and were dedicated entirely to the appreciation of recorded jazz. Its complex nature, designed and conceived as temples of sound, found no similarities elsewhere: they were neither bars in the Western sense nor cafés in the European style. Close Instead, in jazz kissa , conversation was minimal, the record player was sacred, and music was played on high-fidelity equipment at volumes that demanded full attention. Originating after the Second World War, kissa provided a haven for serious listeners who could not afford records or audio systems of their own. Over decades, their interiors developed a distinct aesthetic — wood-panelled walls, warm lighting, and seating arranged to face the speakers rather than each other — creating a sense of intimacy and deep focus. Close JAÇ HiFi Café reinterprets that philosophy for a contemporary Mediterranean city. The design is warm yet refined, with an emphasis on tactile materials and an atmosphere that feels as familiar as one’s own living room. The space, covering 95 square metres, unfolds in a series of distinct zones, each offering a different relationship with music, people, and the city outside. Close In the lounge area, iconic pieces such as Akari E lamp by Isamu Noguchi and artwork by artist Chidy Wayne welcome the visitors. Further into the bar, a monolithic piece of walnut wood that doubles as a giant speaker cabinet plays both parts, as a functional counter and audio sculpture. The most dramatic element of JAÇ, however, lies toward the rear: a large walnut-wood installation that curves across walls and ceiling to form a semi-enclosed listening alcove. The effect is immersive — a space that seems to embrace the listener, pulling them into a cocoon of warm wood and resonant sound. Close Overall, JAÇ conveys a special closeness, brought by its design and enhanced by the music and the people that enjoy it. With contrasting but matching materials, the space is given its own unique personality, bridging Japanese precision with Mediterranean ease. All accompanied by lighting, shaping the atmosphere and framing shared moments. JAÇ HiFi Café ultimately reimagines the jazz kissa experience for 21st-century Barcelona. It offers a place to slow down, to sit alone or with friends, to discover a song or hear an old favourite in new detail, and to inhabit a space where design, music, and human presence are in perfect balance. items.text: YESS Restaurant — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Food YESS Restaurant “A little bit of effort” (and a whole lot of fire) Photographed by Austin Leis Written by Forde Visser Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share On the morning I met with Junya Yamasaki, chef and partner of YESS restaurant , he arrived with armloads of wild fennel—stalky and open, a tangled supernova exuberance of yellow flowers. Because I had already made a cursory tour of Junya’s online presence, I was not surprised; I knew this activity was not unusual. Close YESS, an izakaya style “progressive Japanese restaurant” (website) opened in 2024 in the Arts District of Los Angeles. That’s the simple version of a more detoured (but no time wasted) trajectory. Junya, from the Japanese region of Kansai, began to map his career(s) through Tokyo, London, and Paris, studying (respectively) politics, photography and fine arts . In Tokyo he had also worked in film, but in Paris a restaurant kitchen job pointed him towards the culinary world, and eventually a return to London to help develop the wildly popular Koya noodle bar, which significantly diversified London’s Japanese food scene with traditional udon and inventive daily specials. Close In addition to Junya’s commitment to the local and seasonal present, he also holds a reverence for change, which has been mightily exercised since the restaurant’s beginnings. This year, between the LA Fires and the immigration dynamics, Los Angeles has been a special test. YESS took a breath, a short pause to ensure a safe environment for everyone, and exhaled with a new invitation, the addition of a lunch menu. As welcoming as an exuberance of flowers. items.title: Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin
items.summary: The post  Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Kissabō Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan On a sunny tree-lined street in Berlin’s Prenzlauer Berg, plum-coloured noren (暖簾) — traditional Japanese split curtains — float gently in the breeze. They mark the doorway to Kissabō , a 16-seat tea bar that its owners, Marcin and Gosia Chelkowski, describe as a space for attention and curiosity. Two years ago, the couple moved to Berlin from Szczecin in Poland to realise an idea that had been brewing across their lives. As Gosia explains, “there wasn’t a specific moment in time that Marcin and I came to tea, it was very gradual.” Marcin continues, “In Poland, we were exposed to a lot of Japanese culture through videos and gaming when we were growing up. My thoughts when I was young were, well, Japanese games are cool, so everything in Japan must be cool! [Laughs] So as soon as we could afford to visit there, we did.” Gosia adds, “Instantly, we felt very at home.” Their first visit to Japan was twelve years ago, and since that fateful trip, they have returned almost every year. “We thought, well, we like it so much here, maybe we shouldn’t waste time visiting or experiencing other things,” Marcin says, Gosia nodding in agreement. It was on these visits that they were first exposed to a culture of tea: from the crisp bottles lining convenience store shelves, to the formal practice of chanoyu (茶の湯) practiced in tea houses. “In Japan, tea is everywhere,” Marcin notes. “But when we began drinking tea, we weren’t really pursuing it with intention. As we continued, we began to develop an understanding of the culture — a curiosity about the practice and the way it is connected to something more meaningful.” They describe their path to opening a tea bar as something like osmosis: every time they visited Japan, they met more and more people related to the world of tea — farmers, teachers, craftspeople — and their interest grew. Neither comes from a hospitality background, but both had reached a point in their careers where they felt the need for change. “We were talking to a friend who has a tea school in Kyoto, and he said something that really vibed with us. He told us that for him, having tea during a tea gathering — what we in the West call a tea ceremony — is like a visit to an onsen, it’s a form of relaxation. You take time out of your day to get there, and you know that it will bring calm and clarity. We found this really interesting and started thinking about tea in this kind of direction.” In The Book of Tea, Okakura Kakuzō wrote that “Tea is more than an idealisation of the form of drinking; it is a religion of the art of life.” Published in 1906, the tea philosopher’s seminal work introduced Western audiences to an understanding of tea as an expression of Japanese aesthetics and spirituality; a practice of attentiveness shaped by its entanglement with Zen Buddhism and Taoist ideas of simplicity, impermanence, and the beauty of the ordinary. The sixteenth-century tea master and cultural reformer Sen no Rikyū refined the developing wabi-cha (侘び茶) tradition, in which tea ceremonies emphasised humility and restraint. "In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music." With this rich history in mind, Marcin notes that tea culture itself can be very broad. “It can be very casual, it can be very simple: it is special in different ways. There are many places you might be afraid to step into because you feel you don’t possess the experience required. We want to remove that ‘knowledge’ barrier and make it easy for everyone to share in our curiosity.” The result is a space that draws from the rich culture of tea houses and ceremonies, but renders it slightly anew. “Beyond appreciation for the craft, the culture, and everything that surrounds it was really the desire to create an easy-going atmosphere. In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music. We thought this idea was great. Why not present the depth of tea in this way?” "We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention." The kissaten tradition offers a useful lens: where the formal tea ceremony demands studied preparation and ritual knowledge, the kissaten asks only that you sit and attend. Kissabō’s name draws on this lineage. Written 喫茶房, it shares its first two characters with kissaten — 喫茶, tea-drinking — but swaps 店, shop, for 房, chamber. A quieter word for a quieter place; and in Berlin, where inner-city neighbourhoods are crowded with VC-backed coffee chains serving thousands of three-euro flat whites, a completely unique hospitality offering. As are Kissabō’s guidelines: lowered voices, no photography or filming of those present without their consent, and the expectation of queueing quietly outside during busy times. “We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention,” Marcin explains. “And since opening, we’ve observed that people really enjoy this — the calming of the space — even if they didn’t have that intention when they arrived.” "Nobody is in a rush when they see how much attention is being put in." When visiting Kissabō, it is easy to see how it elicits such a response. The earthen-toned interior – replete with a custom oakwood tea bar, a communal table, a tatami area, and Noguchi light sculptures – is warm and atmospheric. “Everything kind of blends in, but has a voice of its own,” says Gosia. Their tea offerings – currently matcha, gyokuro, genmaicha, and hōjicha – are sourced from Japan and served alongside non-alcoholic seasonal cocktails and a range of handmade Japanese sweets. “We are very fortunate that people have trusted us with their work, their traditions, their years of culture. It is very humbling, and we are trying to do our best to share it in a proper way: without fuss, without overexplaining, always with proper care. items.title: Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play
items.summary: The post  Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Celeste Asfour Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan In the heart of Berlin, a quiet courtyard sits framed by historic properties that once thrummed with the energy of industry. Here, on the ground floor of a 19th-century building, you’ll find Strom —a café where reverie meets play, conceptualised by Berlin-based architectural multihyphenate Celeste Asfour . Celeste’s early life unfolded in an architectural household. “I grew up completely surrounded by it,” she explains. “As a child, my mum was always dragging me to museums and construction sites.” For a time, such proximity made her hesitant about joining the world of design. “That is, until I realised I was lying to myself,” she laughs. While grounded in architecture, her practice finds form in a range of aesthetic expressions—from interior design to objects and photography. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” She says that this path emerged while studying: “It was at university that I realised I might not want to be an architect in the classical sense, because I had a problem with the scale required. It was always: Building, building, building. New, new, new. And that’s just not how I enjoy working.” Her approach turned to what already exists, to material research, and a combination of old and new. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” In late 2024, she was approached with a proposition that closely aligned with her interests: a to-be-determined café, bar, or bistro set on the ground floor of a historic complex that was once home to Berlin’s earliest and most successful restaurateurs. Today, the 19th-century buildings are populated by a new generation of businesses, start-ups, and studios whose offices overlook a large internal courtyard. “The courtyard is beautiful and so are the buildings,” Celeste notes. “But it is a space that was never really used by the public because it wasn’t activated—you would never walk in and discover it unless you worked there.” "In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal..." This project was determined to change this, and—unusually—Celeste joined at its very inception. “It was quite a different setup,” she recalls, “there was no name, no logo, no website, no branding, no colours.” Working with the founders and Swedish branding and design agency Several, Celeste helped imagine what kind of offering would best serve the location. “In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal,” she adds. “The outcome was really shaped by the process: by the way it began, by the space and its requirements, and by the people that I worked with, and by a desire to have fun with it.” From their early conversations, an idea emerged: a seasonal café for artisanal coffee, small plates, and afternoon drinks. A space that would transform the courtyard from a place of transit to one of gathering and encounter. The courtyard has three entrances through which people stream in and out of each day—this perpetual circulation animates the area and renders it a kind of “safe harbour,” says Celeste. From here came the café’s name: Strom translates from German as “electrical current” or “stream”: a flow of people and energy. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture." The graphic identity embraces these ideas. Playful and minimal, its refined sensibility bounces across the webpage and stacks atop itself in the logo. This concept is given physical form by Celeste’s interior design, which focuses on spatial arrangement and a balance of materials. “In every project, I think you have to create some sort of tension,” she says. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture. You have to balance hard things with soft things. That kind of tension results in balance.” In Strom, this balance emerges through combining traditional techniques and historic elements with contemporary processes and objects. “A lot of thought went into the textures and materials,” Celeste explains. “We spent a long time selecting the marble and the wood, considering how the colours and forms would work together.” The rich darkness of the oiled cherry wood contrasts with the bright weight of the brutalist-edged rose marble counter. The tension between these elements is counterbalanced by the softness of the locally handmade terracotta tiles covering the floor. These organic materials are complemented by a range of modern finishes that lend the space a distinct character. Brushed-steel shelves, produced by Studio Ultimo alongside the wooden panelling, hold magazines and objects that Celeste sourced from local antique markets. One shelf provides a view into the kitchen, giving guests a small insight into the creation of their plates before they arrive at their tables. Another features a mirrored backing that adds further depth to the space. Milky-hued mauve tabletops, made from recycled polycarbonate ‘Karlite’ by Dutch studio Plasticiet, are grounded by wooden chairs from Form&Refine and bench seats upholstered in Kvadrat fabric. The space features concertina windows that open the café to the courtyard during warmer weather. When the sun is high, they bring ample light into the space. During the winter months, the lighting design is used for aesthetic form and atmospheric effect. Hand-textured Murano sconces from Milan-based studio 6 am cast a warm rose-hued glow across the interior. A Noguchi lamp throws papered light from the shelves, and a faceted pendant by Asca Studio draws the line of sight to the coffee bar below it. Though the interior is undoubtedly elevated, it is not without a sense of play. The bathroom has been completed with a bulbous, bubble-gum pink sink, whi

items.title: TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency
items.summary: The post  TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name TRADER HiFi Images Clemens Poloczek Words Anna Dorothea Ker Hamburg’s growing TRADER constellation stems from founder Vincent von Thien’s wish to offer his city more than another café. TRADER Gallery in the Schanze set the first tone, uniting specialty coffee with art and design. The latest outpost, TRADER HiFi in the city’s Ottensen district, brings von Thien’s interest in sound into clearer focus. Drawn from the lineage of Japanese kissas and tuned to contemporary life, the space shifts between daytime sociability and evening sessions that invite attentive listening. A considered acoustic architecture, a custom sound system and collaborations with design studios across Europe give the small space its distinctive presence. What emerges is a third place where listening becomes a shared daily pleasure. Origins Vincent von Thien’s route to TRADER began years earlier during long stints in Australia during his modelling career. Sydney in 2011 introduced him to a style of café culture he hadn’t encountered at home—in his words, “my first real encounter with the specialty coffee scene.” It left a mark, even though the tools to build something similar in Germany were out of reach at the time. He began with a mobile version, launching Coffee Bike Hamburg with a friend and serving espresso at festivals. When modelling lost its appeal, he returned to the idea of a fixed space. A small unit in the harbor city’s Schanze district became TRADER Gallery, combining coffee with art and a selection of vintage design. von Thien wanted to offer something civic, not only commercial. “A small fusion of specialty coffee and art,” as he puts it; “to give Hamburg something more than just another café around the corner. I liked the idea of offering emerging artists a fair platform.” TRADER Gallery laid the groundwork for what would follow. Its second iteration, TRADER HiFi—opened in Ottensen in September 2025—extends that vision into the field of sound. Culture of Listening TRADER HiFi’s framework comes from Japan’s jazz kissas—listening cafés—of the 1970s, where, as von Thien puts it, “people could listen to music in high-quality sound because they didn’t have the equipment at home.” He matched this with the atmosphere of today’s listening bars, then rethought the model for Hamburg. The café works in two modes. Days are social, shaped by DJs whose sets provide a spirited backdrop to conversation. Evenings shift to focused sessions where the room falls still. “The idea is that for those sessions we ask people not to talk,” von Thien shares. “They’re dedicated to music.” Performances range from live sets to curated record journeys routed directly through the custom sound system. An accompanying beverage program keeps the mood clear-minded. “We don’t serve alcohol, as I want full focus on specialty coffee and music.” Programming Eclecticism Though still young, TRADER HiFi has already welcomed a wide sweep of genres. “We’ve already had world music, ambient, jazz, disco house,” von Thien shares. Artists such as Coco Maria, Barış Kadem and Dounia hint at the range that threads through the programme, alongside recurring sets by Panama.x and others. “What matters is high-quality music and talented people,” von Thien says. The format attracts those looking for a change in pace or setting, and requests arrive from both Hamburg and abroad. “We’re getting lots of requests from DJs, including international ones. It shows there’s a real need here in Hamburg.” As the first listening café in the city, TRADER HiFi gives artists a venue to explore ideas outside the club context. “Many DJs want to break out of their usual musical setting or play in a different environment, maybe even try another genre,” von Thien notes. The only condition is that the set suits the space. “It’s not a party. It should fit the concept, and artists should have freedom to shape the evening as they imagine.” Room for Sound The interior in Ottensen had to support both hospitality and audio without asserting either too strongly. von Thien pursued his vision for a room that settled the senses. “I wanted to create a timeless, grounding space that suits the music, an atmosphere that invites you to linger and feel calm,” he explains. Cork became central to the acoustic design. Burnt cork lines the ceiling of the main listening room, and a required structural beam was enlarged, packed with acoustic wool and wrapped in cork, acting as a central sound absorber. The custom concept grew in partnership with Antwerp-based Studio Corkinho , whose practice draws on the Alentejo’s long tradition of harvesting oak bark and reworking reclaimed cork into objects and spatial elements with a highly sensorial presence. For the sound system, von Thien worked closely with H.A.N.D. HiFi in Berlin. They developed the layout of the horns, booth and supporting speakers, ensuring the acoustic performance sits naturally within the space. With 70 square meters to work with, every decision counted. To define its configuration, von Thien spent in the emptied space, studying how people would move and where sound would settle. “I moved ideas around, thought things through,” he shares. The footprint is compact, so circulation and bar flow had to work intuitively. Collaborators contributed meaningfully to the final environment. Lisbon-based THER created furniture pieces that lend the room its stripped-back clarity, including wooden tables informed by Japanese woodworking techniques and produced with Portuguese carpentry studio Nó Marceneiros . Brussels-based porcelain studio Frizbee Ceramics produced the tableware used throughout the café, and Vitra supported the project with Akari lamps that bring a soft, diffused light to the interior. Von Thien emphasizes the long view that guided his collaborations: “The idea wasn’t to create hype, but to build a place that still works ten years from now.” A Growing Menu Specialty coffee anchors the beverage program at TRADER HiFi. items.title: Hotel of the Week: A New San Sebastián Stay Is Housed Within a Belle Époque Cinema
items.summary:
The reimagined spaces feature sepia interiors, a proscenium arch entrance, and Lotu, a restaurant from chef Andoni Luis Aduriz’s IXO Group, occupying the old horseshoe balcony 
 The post  Hotel of the Week: A New San Sebastián Stay Is Housed Within a Belle Époque Cinema  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: The Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián occupies a former cinema originally built in 1914. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton After four decades as a vacant landmark in the center of San Sebastián, the Palacio Bellas Artes , one of Spain ’s earliest cinemas, has reopened as a hotel . Original architect Ramón Cortázar, a pioneer of Basque design, drew on Paris ’ s Gaumont Palace for the Beaux-Arts building, which opened in 1914 at the height of the city’s Belle Époque. Today, the entrance runs across the former stage and the lobby opens into a double-height space where the orchestra seating once was. The circa-1914 cinema now home to Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián, Curio Collection by Hilton , debuted in July as the brand’s first hotel in the city, a project promoted by SADE , the family firm that has owned the building since 1914. “Restoring the property meant preserving its dome, façade, and original layout while creating a contemporary hotel shaped by its cinematic history,” says Brooke Thomas, brand leader of Hilton’s Curio Collection . The dome, dismantled in 2015, was rebuilt by architect Ignacio Quemada as an exact replica. Isabel López Vilalta and Silvia Cabestany of ILV* , an interior design studio, designed the interiors, drawing on cinematic elements like balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, and repetition to shape the spaces, while light and color intensify at key points through the building, as if a camera were advancing through a sequence. The proscenium arch that once framed the performances is now the front door. “Crossing the proscenium arch becomes a symbolic threshold: from the real world into the world of fiction,” says López Vilalta. Art Deco details abound while the palette nods to the sepia hues of early film. Photo: Courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton The hotel’s color palette of dusty pinks, warm terracotta, and deep burgundy evokes the sepia tones of early films and photographic negatives. Those rich hues appear in the lobby floor made of Spanish marbles Rojo Alicante, a rosy red threaded with white, and Crema Marfil, a soft beige. “Its flowing geometry follows the architecture of the space, creating a pattern reminiscent of a drop falling into water, with ripples spreading outwards,” López Vilalta says. The suspended ceiling repeats the rings in a rosy hue, and a chandelier of textured glass, made with local fabricator Cianco, draws the eye up toward the mezzanine. Similar shades envelop accommodations designed to provoke tranquility, with natural textiles, wood, and stone. The Rojo Alicante marble carries through to the bedside tables and baths—and even to gorgeous marbled tubs in select suites. Other guest quarters nod to the building’s original use with accommodations labeled Amphitheater rooms, spacious Grand Stalls, or Front Box suites, the latter tucked behind the main façade with the grand windows intact. Two Cupula suites—open-plan studios with a mezzanine lounge, a round pink sofa, and a private terrace—sit inside the rebuilt dome. Cupula Suite at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Cupula Suite at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Guest suite at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton All the accommodations at the Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián feature an artwork by from Basque artist Lander Andonegi. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Each accommodation displays a work from Creation: Light, Movement and Gaze , a series of 81 pieces commissioned from Basque artist Lander Andonegi. “We wanted the art to be part of the building’s new life rather than simply decoration added to it,” she says. Cinematic history also informs the hotel’s restaurant Lotu , which means “to tie” in Basque. A nod to the early 20th-century dining rooms where actors, writers and filmmakers gathered between premieres, the restaurant serves pâté en croûte, sole meunière and a beef Wellington in the style of La Tour d’Argent, alongside txangurro donostiarra, the classic Basque stuffed spider crab, and a Singaporean black pepper crab. Overseen by chef Andoni Luis Aduriz and his IXO Grupo , it’s the latest destination for the team which also runs Mugaritz , a two-Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant in nearby Errenteria built on experimental and avant-garde gastronomy. Lotu at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Lotu at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Lotu at Hotel Palacio Bellas Artes San Sebastián. Photo: courtesy of Curio Collection by Hilton Between atmospheric surroundings, star-powered cuisine, and a film-inspired soundtrack, the hotel has all the glamour of its original heyday while still preserving the authentic flavor of the city. “The care that went into the hotel’s design makes the hotel feel rooted in San Sebastián,” suggests Thomas, “as if it could only exist there.” Tags: Art Deco Hotels Restaurants Spain

items.title: Pensão Amor  in Lisbon, Portugal
items.summary:

items.text: About Walk down Pink Street in Lisbon’s Cais do Sodré and you’ll eventually find a door that looks like it has secrets. Pensão Amor building is a former brothel that has been transformed into a surprising space in Lisbon's port district. Cais do Sodré was once the sailors’ quarter, where seamen fresh off the boats mingled with writers, fado singers, artists, prostitutes and the occasional spy. Pensão Amor takes that cast of characters and gives them a party. The bar is a riot of velvet, red light, and cheerful mischief. On any given night, you might catch burlesque, pole dancing, live music, poetry, or theater, sometimes all in the same week. Nobody here is trying to hide what the building used to be. They hung it on the wall. Other surprise is upstairs. In 2023, the old brothel floors reopened as Madam’s Lodge, a 22-room hotel with a twist: every room has its own invented backstory. Screenwriter and director Roger Mor wrote each one, drawing on archival research and objects tied to the building and the neighborhood. Illustrator Nuno Saraiva drew the characters and left his mark across the building, so even the walls seem to have opinions. Some rooms also come with pole dancing bars, strategically placed mirrors, bathtubs made for two, and minibars stocked with adult goodies. items.text: About There are plenty of creatures to spot along Dublin's River Dodder, but few walkers expect to encounter a rhinoceros. Standing on a plinth in the middle of the river near Classon's Bridge is a remarkably lifelike, life-size bronze rhino that has become one of Milltown's strangest landmarks. The animal appeared seemingly overnight in 2002, with no plaque explaining who created it, who put it there, or why a rhinoceros was chosen. Contemporary reports noted that nobody had claimed responsibility, and the nearby Dropping Well pub denied being behind its mysterious arrival. The pub nevertheless embraced its unusual neighbour, even running a competition to give the creature a name. Suggestions included “Rhino O'Neal,” “The Plodder in the Dodder,” and “The Milltown Muddler.” The Dodder itself soon added to the mystery. During flooding in November 2002, the rhino disappeared beneath the swollen river, leaving Dubliners waiting for the water to fall to discover whether their new resident had survived. It did, and more than two decades later the bronze beast is still standing watch over the Dodder. Today, spotting the rhino is one of the more surreal surprises on a walk along the river. Its creator and the full story of how it arrived remain uncertain, leaving Dublin with a piece of public art whose mystery is almost as memorable as the sculpture itself. Know Before You Go The rhino stands in the River Dodder beside The Dropping Well pub in Milltown, just upstream of Classon's Bridge. It can be seen from the riverside path behind the pub, so there is no need to enter the pub to spot it. Milltown Luas stop is a short walk away. For the best view, follow the path along the northern bank of the Dodder toward Classon's Bridge and look out into the river.
