No traffic, no reservations, no problem. I’m Nora Ritchie, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side. This month, we’re talking with Canadian writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, I’m talking with Andrew Phung. Andrew is a comedian and actor best known for playing Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience , and he’s the creator and star of Run the Burbs . But for this conversation, what matters most is that Andrew is a superfan of Calgary, the medium-sized city where he grew up. This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast : a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and all major podcast apps. To Andrew Phung, Calgary is simultaneously a big city and a small town—in all the right ways. Travel Alberta / Sameer Ahmed Calgary is in southern Alberta, where the prairies meet the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. And to be honest, it’s not exactly considered the poster child for Alberta tourism. That honor usually goes to places like Banff and Lake Louise, with their turquoise lakes and mountain views. But Andrew thinks his hometown deserves a little more love. Andrew: I would describe Calgary as a really big city that has all the amenities but feels a bit like a small town at times in regards to its friendliness. The mountains are right behind you. There’s really fresh air, and it is so bright. I think there’s some wild statistic, like Calgary gets the most sunshine in, like, all of the world during the winter or something like that. Nora: I wanna hear about the street you grew up on, your neighborhood. Andrew: I will talk about Northeast Calgary until I die. The northeast of Calgary is a quadrant of the city. It is the most culturally diverse. I grew up in Whitehorn, Temple, Falconridge, Coral Springs. I’ll name the neighborhoods, but Coral Springs was where we ended up last. And what I loved about it was, Coral Springs is full of dreamers. It’s people who this was the first new house they bought. And it was really affordable to new immigrants, families starting out fresh. So literally everyone on my street had kids, and so we were always playing. Like, every day after school, we’d come home, we would get on our bikes, we would go to someone’s house, get the baseball equipment, get the hockey equipment, carry the net, you know, all that stuff. Every day at 5:00, you know, people would come home from work, and then we’d have to go inside and have dinner and do homework. That was our street. It felt a little bit like Pleasantville. Nora: It does sound like Pleasantville. So your parents are Chinese and Vietnamese. How did they end up in Calgary? Andrew: So most people assume your parents come to Canada together. My parents met in Canada. They had different immigration stories. My mom immigrated to Airdrie, Alberta, which is a suburb of Calgary. My dad ended up in Saskatchewan. A church there had sponsored a bunch of Vietnamese refugees into Canada. And then my dad tracked down a friend living in Calgary, and he went to take the bus to Calgary and waited for him at the bus station, and the guy didn’t show up. And then my dad saw another person delivering Chinese food, went and talked to that guy, and that guy took my dad home, and my dad lived with him for two years. The Asian community in Calgary in the ’70s and ’80s was so tight-knit. Like, if they saw one of their own, they would take you in. It was so supportive. And I remember years later, my dad saw an old friend. I’m like, “Yo, who was that guy?” My dad’s like, “Oh, I used to live with him.” And I’m like, “You need to give me the full backstory on that.” But my mom and dad met in Airdrie at a card game. My uncle introduced my mom and dad, and I was born and raised in Calgary. That’s our immigration story, and I really always reflect on how welcoming Canada was in the ’70s and ’80s. Really welcoming in refugees and immigrants to build a better life. And my parents always say, “Andrew, we’re living the Canadian dream. items.title: Anchorage: A City Within the Wild
items.summary:
In  Anchorage , exploring nature isn’t only for a rare free day or a well-planned vacation; it’s a part of daily life, as integral to the city as its infrastructure and cultural offerings. A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales.

A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales. Located on a coastal plain that shifts into alpine slopes farther east, Anchorage is unique in how its different ecosystems overlap, creating rich diversity in wildlife, botany, and geology. You can experience the best of nature while still enjoying all the creature comforts of urban life and stumble across breathtaking sights without even looking for them. In this guide, we’ve given you some starting points for exploring the wild from Alaska’s biggest city, with wonders ranging from undisturbed wooded trails to marshes that all kinds of animals call home. Ready to take a walk on the wild side? Fishing season runs roughly from late May to early September. Wayde Carroll for Visit Anchorage Ship Creek This 25-mile-long river flows from the Chugach Mountains down into the Port of Alaska on Anchorage’s northern side, where it’s become a popular spot for sport fishing and bird watching. Thanks to its mud and sedge flats, and ocean-fed waters, this area is home to a massive annual run of coho and Chinook salmon. In fact, it’s the only urban Chinook fishery in the world. The 5.8-mile Ship Creek Trail is a perfect way to spend time in nature without leaving the city limits, providing views of salmon spawning and swimming upstream during the summer. Stops along the way, like Ship Creek Overlook Park and the pedestrian bridge just off King’s Landing, provide especially great panoramas of the river and the surrounding mountains. It’s not uncommon to see anglers trying their luck for 20- to 30-pound salmon, and you can even visit the statue of Dena’ina matriarch Grandma Olga , fish filets in her hands and a bronze drying rack behind her. The trail’s namesake is a former Anchorage mayor and Alaska governor. Chris Arend for Visit Anchorage Tony Knowles Coastal Trail For a longer walk, try this 11-mile path that stretches from downtown Anchorage all the way to the Kincaid Park Chalet. However, if you’re looking for a shorter trek, have no fear: The trail is accessible from multiple points in the city, meaning you can hop on or off. You don’t have to explore on foot either, as the trail can be traversed easily by bike and, in the winter, cross-country skis. No matter how you travel the trail, you’re guaranteed some incredible views of downtown Anchorage, Mount McKinley (Denali), Mount Susitna, and Fire Island, especially as you reach the hills near Point Woronzof. The trail offers a rare chance to pass through a number of different biomes, as it winds through marsh, muskeg (acidic, waterlogged peatland), and thick spruce forest. There’s also plenty of wildlife nearby, with moose, in particular, enjoying long walks on the path during the winter. Other animals often spotted include sandhill cranes, ermine, bald eagles, and even beluga whales in Cook Inlet, so don’t forget your camera. Trails rising from the sand dunes and following the bluffs provide some of the best views in Kincaid Park. Paxson Woelber via Flickr CC BY 2.0 Kincaid Park For even more great hiking, visit Kincaid Park, a 1,400-acre green space that was once a Cold War missile base. There’s plenty to do in Kincaid: walk down the 40 miles of cleared trails, practice archery on a designated range, paddle through Little Campbell Lake, or play disc golf on an 18-hole course. There are also seven different soccer fields, a motocross course, and a giant sand dune with stunning views of Cook Inlet and the Kenai Peninsula. In the winter, the park becomes a premier destination for sledding and cross-country skiing, with trails for every skill level. The marsh’s many overlapping habitats make it a hub for all kinds of wildlife. Jody O. Photos for Visit Anchorage Potter Marsh Just 15 minutes south of downtown, this part of the Anchorage Coastal Wildlife Refuge is one of the best wildlife viewing spots in all of Alaska, offering sweeping vistas of the Turnagain Arm tidal waterway and half a mile of boardwalk across the channels and sedges. This wetland ecosystem is full of creatures big and small, from muskrats paddling through the water to the occasional moose taking a dip. And birders, rejoice: The marsh is home to more than 130 bird species, including Arctic tern, Canada geese, trumpeter swans, red-necked grebes, and northern pintails. Pro tip: Visit in April for the greatest variety of migrating birds, or in midsummer to see three different species of salmon schooling under the boardwalk. Information panels and telescopes along the path make it easy to enjoy a self-guided tour and take in the sights and sounds of the marsh at your own pace. You can also see the marsh from aboard the Alaska Railroad or while driving down the Seward Highway . Beluga Point is also a significant archaeological site, with artifacts 8,000 to 10,000 years old. Monica Whitt for Visit Anchorage Beluga Point Also along the Seward Highway sits Beluga Point, a rocky promontory named for the population of beluga whales that can be spotted each July and August when they come to catch salmon in the inlet. However, no matter what time of year you visit, 180-degree views of the Chugach Mountains make this a worthwhile place to stop and take in your surroundings. items.title: Dorothee Meilichzon
items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu COWLEY MANOR Cotswolds Cowley, Cheltenham GL53 9NL, Royaume-Uni july 2023 Built in 1695, this manor changed hands several times before James Horlick acquired it in 1895. Together with the next owner, Colonel Heber Percy, he oversaw most of the building’s transformations. Now converted into a hotel, the manor also features stables, a contemporary extension and a large spa. It offers 36 rooms, alongside a wealth of living and social spaces: a garden room, a games room, a cocktail bar, a cocktail lounge, a restaurant, a library, a mudroom and two swimming pools, among others. Our intention was to do what we love most: bring together geometric elements, mix styles and eras, and celebrate the many transformations the buildings have undergone, from 1695 to the 2000s. The result is, ultimately, a delightful joyeux bordel — a beautifully eclectic mix of styles, periods and ideas. Our main source of inspiration was, of course, the building itself. We combined classical references, paying tribute to the original manor, with canopy beds, figured maple, verdigris finishes and sophisticated rattan furniture, alongside contemporary elements such as enamelled lava stone, lime-plastered walls, boldly graphic fabrics and carpets, fully upholstered furniture, vibrant colours, glossy lacquer and, above all, an abundance of checkerboard patterns! These patterns were also a nod to Alice in Wonderland . Lewis Carroll wrote Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland while staying at Cowley Manor, inspired by its grounds. As a playful wink to this story, we incorporated hidden little doors and subtle references to Alice throughout the interiors. Checkerboard patterns appear everywhere: on rugs and carpets, across fabrics and painted walls, in varying scales and colours, from tone-on-tone combinations to sculpted surfaces and enamelled lava stone. items.title: Dorothee Meilichzon
items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu HOTEL REGINA biarritz 52 Av. de l'Impératrice, 64200 Biarritz July 2023 Perched on a cliff in Biarritz, overlooking Cap Saint-Martin and the Atlantic Ocean, the Hôtel Regina has stood proudly for nearly 120 years. Built as a hotel in 1906 by architect Henry Martinet, the building is a remarkable example of Belle Époque architecture. This period naturally became our starting point, with its impressive 15-metre-high atrium, grand windows and sculpted architectural details. We also wanted to draw inspiration from local architectural styles of the same period, particularly Neo-Basque architecture. The work of the Gómez brothers, especially Villa Malaye, served as a reference, alongside Villa Leïhorra by Joseph Hiriart and Villa Arnaga by Albert Tournaire. These influences informed a vocabulary of white architecture, semicircular forms, sculpted frescoes, fluted cornices, 45-degree angles, tiled génoises , semicircular mirrors, black wrought iron and Art Deco stoneware tiles by Winckelmans. We also drew inspiration from the Atlantic Ocean itself: rope-inspired mouldings and skirting boards, striped fabrics, dark and pale blue lacquer finishes, ocean-liner architecture, bathroom vanities echoing the shape of a pelota pediment, and fabrics draped like sails. And, of course, shells! Razor clams are sculpted into the reception desk, while marine life appears in wall lights, carpets, fabrics and bas-reliefs. We also wanted to pay tribute to Japan and its close historical and cultural ties with the Basque Country. Japanese straw, black lacquer, indigo-dyed hanging fabrics and paper lanterns all contribute to this dialogue between cultures. The result is a luminous, layered interior where dark green, deep red and shades of blue are balanced by stoneware, ceramics and natural materials such as straw and rope. The rooms are predominantly white, blue and mint green, with undulating génoises , panelled doors, wardrobes clad in Japanese straw and rope details, and oversized headboards finished in pale blue lacquer. The corridors open onto the grand atrium and feature carpets printed with aquatic motifs. The spa combines pale blue and warm green tones, curved tiles, lime-plastered walls and straw wallcoverings. The restaurant and atrium take inspiration from the architectural language of Eileen Gray in the late 1920s. Curved wooden furniture, her iconic bar stools and a counter inspired by her house at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin evoke the streamlined elegance of a grand ocean liner. Within the atrium, we have created a series of intimate sitting areas, furnished with suspended paper lights by Ingo Maurer and Anthony Dickens, alongside sofas inspired by the forms of the Itsasoan bridge in Guéthary. Built as a hotel in 1906 by architect Henry Martinet, the building is a remarkable example of Belle Époque architecture. This period naturally became our starting point, with its impressive 15-metre-high atrium, grand windows and sculpted architectural details. We also wanted to draw inspiration from local architectural styles of the same period, particularly Neo-Basque architecture. The work of the Gómez brothers, especially Villa Malaye, served as a reference, alongside Villa Leïhorra by Joseph Hiriart and Villa Arnaga by Albert Tournaire. These influences informed a vocabulary of white architecture, semicircular forms, sculpted frescoes, fluted cornices, 45-degree angles, tiled génoises , semicircular mirrors, black wrought iron and Art Deco stoneware tiles by Winckelmans. items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu Gran Hotel MONTESOL Ibiza Passeig de Vara de Rey - Ibiza - Balearic Islands - Spain april 2023 Following the renovation of Sabbaba restaurant and its rooftop in 2021, we went on to renovate the rooms of this legendary Ibiza hotel, the first to open on the island. Dating back to 1933, the building features a Neo-Colonial architectural style, with columns, pediments and arches painted in pale yellow and white. For the interiors, we developed a colour palette that echoes the pale yellow of the façade while drawing on Ayurvedic principles. To counterbalance the heat outside, we introduced cooler, calming colours throughout the hotel: solar tones in the communal areas and lunar hues in the bedrooms, with shades of white, blue, grey, pale green and soft pastels. We embraced Ibiza’s bohemian spirit through an abundance of fabrics, patterns, fringes and pompoms, pairing them with light wood, colourful rugs and richly textured walls. We even created a bespoke shell-textured wall finish for the hotel, pressing seashells into the lime plaster by hand, one by one. The hotel is bursting with colour, reflecting the joy and tolerance that define Ibiza. Cosmic shapes and playful details appear throughout the interiors. In every room, an oversized moon is carved into the wall, creating an opening between the bedroom and the bathroom. We designed iron chairs featuring a moon motif, added brass suns to the walls and introduced wavy lines throughout the spaces. Other distinctive details include handmade masks by Anna Alexandra in Mallorca and the Playdough stool by Diego Faivre. Tiles also play an important role in the design. Traditional zellige tiles in shades of orange, brown and off-white line the minibar niches. The wardrobe doors feature interlocking jigsaw-puzzle shapes and a high-gloss lacquer finish. The bathroom vanities are made from French lava stone and paired with generously proportioned, sculptural mirrors in walnut and lacquer — and, of course, a few little pompoms to complete the look. items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu IL PALAZZO experimental Venezia Fondamenta Zattere, Dorsoduro, Venezia, VE 30123 2019 Il Palazzo Experimental is housed in Ca’ Molin, a historic palazzo that later became the headquarters of Adriatica, a maritime transport company, until its closure. Located along the Zattere waterfront in the Dorsoduro district of Venice, the palazzo has two points of access: one facing the Giudecca Canal and another via a private pier on the Rio de Ognissanti. The hotel features 33 rooms, a restaurant with a terrace overlooking the Giudecca Canal, a garden terrace and a cocktail bar. We designed the interiors of the hotel and restaurant by combining the traditional Venetian elements we love with more contemporary influences, including references to the Memphis movement, bold colours, brushed aluminium, scalloped edges, glass lighting by Luciano Vistosi, Breccia Capraia marble and arches framing the bathtubs. We preserved as many of the palazzo’s original architectural features as possible: the exposed beams, the impressive ceiling height on the first floor, the gallery, the magnificent Gothic windows and the double wooden doors. These existing elements already possess a strong identity, which we sought to enhance through a rich Venetian vocabulary: symmetrical compositions, marble surfaces, stripes in many forms — painted, in metal marquetry or in fabrics — references to gothique fleuri , and colours inspired by the lagoon and Venetian façades. We also embraced traditional Venetian craftsmanship and timeless techniques, including black lacquer, traditional Venetian cement terrazzo, and marmorino and calce finishes on the walls. The restaurant occupies a generous space on the ground floor. A counter near the entrance welcomes guests with wines, Spritz and cicchetti , while an open kitchen at the back of the room is set behind a large counter. The interiors have a timeless feel, combining a monumental marble plinth, furniture inspired by lits-bateaux , abundant fabrics, antique-inspired details, stripes and terrazzo in the spirit of Carlo Scarpa. A pale green ceiling evokes the lagoon, while shades of white, salmon pink, burgundy and pale green complete the palette. For the cocktail bar, I invited my friend, architect Cristina Celestino, to develop the interior design and create a distinctively Venetian atmosphere of her own. items.title: Dorothee Meilichzon
items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu HOTEL MENORCA experimental Sant Llorenç - Menorca - Balearic Islands - Spain 2019 43 rooms, 1 vegetable garden, 9 private houses with swimming pools, 1 indoor restaurant and cocktail bar, 30 hectares, 1 large outdoor swimming pool, 1 poolside cocktail bar, 1 outdoor restaurant… Menorca Experimental is a 30-hectare estate near Alaior, Menorca, imagined as the summer residence of an artist who exists only in our imagination. Just as Miró found inspiration in Mallorca, Dalí in Cadaqués, and Picasso on the French Riviera, this is a place devoted to drawing, contemplation, meditation, music, swimming, watching the sunset and, above all, taking the time to do nothing, surrounded by an extraordinary landscape. The overall aesthetic of the hotel was conceived as an invitation to creativity and inspiration. Dorothée Meilichzon and her team began by drawing on Menorca’s traditional craftsmanship and local materials: stone, built-in concrete furniture, terracotta, semicircular forms, architraves, wooden shutters, leather and reclaimed materials from the estate’s former farm buildings, including wooden beams, roof tiles and marès stone. These elements were combined with distinctive details and bespoke designs: colourful door architraves, rounded concrete headboards and bathroom vanities, vibrant combinations of cement and lacquer, terracotta, and handmade glazed tiles. The furniture was crafted by local artisans on the island, following Dorothée’s designs. Dorothée also collaborated with a number of talented creatives to create a unique, handcrafted experience in Menorca: KAREL BALAS created all the graphic elements, including a hand-drawn alphabet and a series of illustrations inspired by the ink drawings of Miró and Picasso. LRNCE designed a collection of bespoke handwoven blankets, made in Marrakech exclusively for the hotel. Their illustrations echo Karel’s drawings and Dorothée’s colour palette. Léa Munsch hand-shaped large-scale light fixtures from a specially developed clay, working from Dorothée’s designs. The outdoor spaces are an essential part of the project. We preserved the local plant species, allowing nature to continue reclaiming the estate and maintaining its original character. A vegetable garden supplies the restaurant and cocktail bar with fresh fruit and vegetables, further connecting the project to its landscape and its Mediterranean roots. items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu HOTEL des GRANDS BOULEVARDS Paris 17 bvd Poissonnière - Paris II 2018 Back when the Grands Boulevards were still a leafy promenade and the French Revolution was in full swing in 1789, this private mansion was built. Three centuries later, the Hôtel des Grands Boulevards was born. The rooms play with the splendour of the period: canopy beds, glass-fronted cupboards and red marble, much loved by Louis XVI, are paired with a more rustic aesthetic — antique linen, textured plaster walls, weathered wooden furniture and bronze wall sconces with a beautifully aged patina. Set between the street and an inner courtyard, the hotel reveals itself only after passing through the building’s entrance porch. A hidden retreat, a little secret tucked away from the bustle of the city. It is home to a generous restaurant led by Giovanni Passerini and an intimate cocktail bar beloved by the Experimental Group. Set back from the street, as was customary at the time, the building offers a wealth of terraces and courtyards in which to gather and unwind. An outdoor bar, yoga classes, lush greenery and open-air grills bring these spaces to life, blurring the boundaries between indoors and out. items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu HENRIETTA hotel London 14/15 Henrietta St - Covent Garden - London 2017 The Henrietta Hotel was my first hotel project in London, and my fourth project in the city with the Experimental Group. The hotel features 18 rooms and a restaurant led by chef Ollie Dabbous. My first source of inspiration was the street itself. I always try to begin with the neighbourhood. On Henrietta Street, the buildings are very traditional, with understated façades, yet an extraordinary variety of rooflines and window ornamentation. Each building has its own rich and distinctive character. This reminded me of classical architectural ornamentation — arches, capitals and bas-reliefs — as well as the magnificent door surrounds often found in Milanese apartments. Inspired by these references, I designed oversized headboards conceived as bas-reliefs, combining different elements: mirrors, fabric panels upholstered in Rubelli fabrics, and hand-painted patterns, all assembled by hand. The doors are topped with decorative capitals, and a glazed capital separates the bathroom from the bedroom. For the bedroom carpets, I designed a pattern inspired by the shapes of mosaïque casson , while all the skirting boards are made from white Carrara marble. Four distinct colour schemes bring individuality to the hotel’s 18 rooms, ensuring that each has its own character. The bedside lights are made of brass and rise unusually high, integrated into the bedside tables. As I often enjoy mixing styles and periods, I also introduced references to the 1970s, designing a small armchair inspired by Pierre Paulin’s work and incorporating brushed aluminium details. In the bathrooms, the vanity area was conceived as a fountain: two large pieces of granite meet at a right angle, creating a sculptural form inspired by the architecture of one of the buildings on Henrietta Street. A large mirror rests above this composition. The flooring offers a more traditional touch, with black-and-white octagonal tiles and cabochons. * HENRIETTA HOTEL HAS BEEN SHORTLISTED IN THE BEST URBAN HOTELS BY WALLPAPER IN 2017* Client : Experimental Group Chef : Italian Supper club Interior Architecture + Design : Dorothee Meilichzon Graphic Design : Dorothee Meilichzon Photos : Karel Balas & Paul Bowyer HENRIETTA hotel London 14/15 Henrietta St - Covent Garden - London 2017 The Henrietta Hotel was my first hotel project in London, and my fourth project in the city with the Experimental Group. items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu hotel PANACHE Paris 20 rue du Faubourg Montmartre - PARIS IX 2016 The Hotel Panache was inspired by both its neighbourhood and the building itself. Shaped like New York’s iconic Flatiron Building, it became the starting point for a design built around angles and geometry. Triangular mirrors, geometric patterns on the carpets, walls and mosaics — even the wardrobes are tucked into corners. Nothing is square, except the bed! The turn of the century, or Art Nouveau , was another major source of inspiration. I designed bas-reliefs and curved headboards inspired by the turned wood and sculptural forms of traditional Art Nouveau furniture. The hotel also features a restaurant on the ground floor, with David Lanher at the helm. items.title: Meet Islyn - Islyn
items.text: Meet Islyn - Islyn Projects All Projects Interior Design Branding In Development About Press & Awards Journal Contact Islyn Studio New York, NY Instagram Follow Us @islynstudio #islynstudio VIEW ALL POSTS 17.05.2023 Like the Islyn of our namesake, Islyn Studio believes in the stories behind things. We are not afraid to fail. We are not afraid to jump off cliffs into blue waters. We are not afraid of things we haven’t seen before. Or in the imperfect. We believe in learning by doing. We are good listeners. Our eyes are open and our hearts are wild. If we can, for a second, remind someone of a world that’s bigger and greater than the ones they’ve seen, then we’ve done our jobs. Meet Islyn Islyn doesn’t remember much about the boat ride from Sicily, only that she sat under her mother’s skirt and ate red tomatoes from a cloth sack, the juice sticky and dripping on her bare legs. Islyn’s parents were archaeologists, so they believed in the stories behind things, and taught her to, as well. As an only child, she grew up with her own imagination to sustain her, and the small, daily pleasures of life on Earth. She loved the sound of keys clacking and of men’s dress shoes on terrazzo. On hot days in Puglia, she wore that one particular white linen dress (the one with the open back), and leaned against marble in the piazza (you could tell it was real marble because it was so cold even though the day was so hot). She would go to the flea market and learn about the way objects conferred meaning. She could feel, in an antique bronze cup, the wild histories of those who’d touched it before. She collected leather saddles and green glass from Turkish coasts that grazed her windowsills. She pressed Kyoto’s cherry blossoms between the pages of her journal and gathered bone-white wood from the New Mexican desert. As a teen, she drank warm beer with locals in highway Cambodian bars and walked through Roman ruins at dusk. She rode horses bareback in Kentucky and stopped to listen to violinists, neon-lit in New York subways. She knew all the names of the wildflowers on the Eastern seaboard. She dove from the red cliffs of Sardinia. Her lipstick was smudged, her hair was messy. She was effortlessly cool. She loved old cars with brown leather interiors, and vowed never to dye her hair once it went gray. Islyn liked the way she could tell time in photographs by how long the shadows were. She liked when someone missed a spot shaving. She loved incense in cold stone churches and baskets of hibiscus flowers in Mexican groceries. She loved people, and wanted their lives to be as rich and beautiful as hers had been. So she built worlds for them. Sometimes this meant a house. Sometimes it meant a drink. Sometimes it meant a well-worn and passionate story about her travels. Whatever it was, she did it with her whole heart. Never cliche. Never boring. Always open and kind and with a lust for life and ideas. Like the Islyn of our namesake, Islyn Studio believes in the stories behind things. We are not afraid to fail. We are not afraid to jump off cliffs into blue waters. We are not afraid of things we haven’t seen before. Or in the imperfect. We believe in learning by doing. We are good listeners. Our eyes are open and our hearts are wild. If we can, for a second, remind someone of a world that’s bigger and greater than the ones they’ve seen, then we’ve done our jobs. PREVIOUS POST NEXT POST

W Hotel Times Square ‍ New York | Hotel Defiant Debut Positioning the hotel as the premier destination to define the direction for W Project Details date 2001 Services Interiors Styling Art Advisory Custom Product Design Lighting Client Starwood Hotels & Resorts Brand W Hotels Region North America Typology Hotel Architect Frank Williams & Partners Architects Location Low Point ‍ The W was built on the site of a failed Planet Hollywood hotel during the aftermath of the dot-com crash and just months after 9/11, at a time when Times Square had become a place many New Yorkers avoided. ‍ Durable Novelty ‍ The goal was simple: to be dramatic without becoming spectacle. Dim lighting, reflective surfaces, and immersive textures created an atmosphere that was both intimate and electric. It established a new modern, minimalist definition of luxury—clean architectural lines paired with rich, moody tones and distinctive materials. ‍ Experience Elemental ‍ The design blurred the boundaries between hospitality, nightlife, and art, positioning the hotel as one of the first lifestyle destinations that offered an experience instead of just accommodation. Reception was located on the seventh floor, creating the atmosphere of a private club rather than a public common space. W Times Square drew New Yorkers in with nightlife that erased the lines between the city and the hotel. ‍ Sensory Driven Design ‍ The tunnel entrance has water cascading down on either side of guests to wash away the chaos outside. ''The idea was to create a sensual, cocoonlike, pared-down antidote to the frenetic pace of Times Square,'' - Glenn Pushelberg. ‍ Formula Foundations ‍ This project proved that a hotel in a hyper-commercial neighborhood could feel both exclusive and immersive. Reaching occupancy targets within its first months, the concept demonstrated a winning formula. W went on to develop more than 70 hotels, with our foundational elements forming the core of its brand design guide. ‍ Drag Click to play “The opening of the W New York–Times Square flagship marks another huge coup for this brand. We are pleased to debut our flagship property in the world’s most exhilarating neighborhood, central to all that is New York City—the excitement, the diversity and the uniqueness.” Barry Sternlicht (former CEO of Starwood) Related spaces Explore The Detroit Edition Residences Detroit Explore Miami Tropic Residences Miami Explore Hotel The Mitsui Hakone Japan Explore 255 East 77th Street New York City Explore Onuki Athens Athens Join our newsletter Thank you! La Samaritaine ‍ Paris | Retail Second Coming Breathing new life into a classic by bringing the feel of Parisian streets indoors Project Details date 2021 Services Interiors Custom Product Design Client LVMH Brand La Samaritaine Region Europe Typology Retail Architect Kazuyo Sejima & Ryue Nishizawa) Great Expectations ‍ Opened in 1870 by a modest salesman, “La Sam’s” growing popularity led architect Frantz Jourdain to convince the family to commission a new iron-framed Art Nouveau building in 1910, bringing art into the streets of Paris. In 1928, the retail space expanded with Henri Sauvage’s Art Deco extension. When LVMH acquired the four timeworn buildings in 2005, the challenge was how to preserve their storied heritage while breathing new life into them. Creative Constraints ‍ Redesigning the Art Nouveau interior, now known as the Pont Neuf side, presented the challenge of harmonizing with the expressive, heritage-protected architecture rather than overshadowing it. Over Indexing ‍ The original brief targeted foreign tourists, but we rethought the idea, knowing that visitors come to experience the authenticity of Paris and French culture. Rather than designing something to appeal to a global audience, we found that imbuing the space with local references would resonate more deeply with those from afar by creating a stronger sense of place. Discovery Center ‍ Inspired by The Flâneur, Edmund White’s book on Paris, the building’s shallow floor plates naturally support a spatial layout that encourages strolling rather than the cavernous aisles and mission-driven shopping typical of multibrand stores found in airports. Bonding Brands ‍ Inspired by the building’s architecture, we designed fixtures that guide the shopping experience subtly - integrated yet unobstructive. With fine, subtle detailing, the fixtures create a cohesive backdrop for the merchandise and support LVMH’s portfolio of brands—each with a distinct voice—coming together as an ensemble cast on a stage that already carries strong character. items.title: Vesper Bar at The Dorchester, London — MBDS
items.text: LONDON Vesper Bar at The Dorchester Formerly the Bar at Dorchester, the newly named Vesper Bar opened in 2022 in London’s legendary Dorchester Hotel. Inspired by the artists of the Roaring Twenties, we wanted to infuse the spirit of this landmark bar with a glamorous feel. Martin Brudnizki The style takes its inspiration from typical of interiors in the 1920s, with a palladium leaf ceiling, sienna marble bar, intricate timber marquetry panels alongside mirrored columns that make the space glow. Bright young things A series of Cecil Beaton drawings feature on the walls to remind guests of the hotel’s elegant past. Selected works

items.title: Nubeluz at the Ritz Carlton, New York — MBDS
items.text: Nubeluz at the Ritz Carlton, New York — MBDS 0 NEW YORK Nubeluz at the Ritz Carlton Nubeluz is a bar located in the Ritz Carlton Nomad New York by José Andrés. The interior is a lightbox in the sky, bringing together the Spanish word for cloud (“nube”) and for light (“luz”). A clean and streamlined approach was taken to the interiors, with bold, organic forms. Martin Brudnizki Selected works Previous Previous Vesper Bar at The Dorchester, London Next Next Chiki, Mexico

items.title: Chiki, Mexico — MBDS
items.text: Chiki, Mexico — MBDS 0 COSTA PALMAS, MEXICO Chiki’s Hidden down an unassuming alleyway bordered by luscious palms, Chiki’s is a private members’ club that offers a contemporary take on the old-world cantinas of Mexico. La Casa Azul inspired us, the idea of a gathering place and a style that is eclectic but grounded in Mexican culture. Martin Brudnizki Selected works Previous Previous Nubeluz at the Ritz Carlton, New York Next Next Annabel's, London

items.title: Annabel's, London — MBDS
items.text: London Annabel’s Annabel's is a private members’ club situated in a Grade-I Listed Georgian Townhouse on London’s Berkeley Square. The new building’s garden and verdant greenery of Berkeley Square and the spirit of English eccentricity. Martin Brudnizki Taking inspiration from the new building’s garden and verdant greenery of Berkeley Square and the spirit of English eccentricity , the new Annabel’s communicates a design which draws direct links to flora and fauna in an eclectic and playful manner. Each floor of the four-storey Georgian townhouse tells a unique story, based upon various gardens depicted throughout history, all whilst paying homage to the original architectural detailing of the listed building. A Verdant Escape Georgian splendor fuses with whimsical English eccentricity, celebrating botanical grandeur in a delightful members club. Selected works

items.title: Soho Beach House, Miami — MBDS
items.text: Miami Soho Beach House Described as the place where ‘grit meets glamour, hotel meets private club,’ Soho Beach House is located on Collins Avenue in the Mid-Beach area of Miami. The oceanfront hotel, channels Cuba and Latin America for its inspiration. Martin Brudnizki The hotel has a Cuban and Latin American-inspired design , incorporating salvaged timber, vintage furniture, and reclaimed fixtures. The design features a faded colour palette and aged timbers reminiscent of the maritime and Old Havana , paired with colourful mosaics, modern details, and an eclectic mix of vintage pieces. The hotel's suites feature unique vintage pieces sourced from antique dealers on the West Coast of America , while the bathrooms are designed in a classic British style. American Beach Luxury. Casual elegance meets vintage charm in this oceanfront Cuban-inspired haven. Selected works

items.title: The Beekman, New York — MBDS
items.text: New York The Beekman The Beekman is a 287 room Thompson Hotel located near Manhattan’s Financial District. The Beekman is a hotel with history and provenance. Its interiors tell this story. Martin Brudnizki Originally called Temple Court and built in 1881 in the American Queen Anne style , the rich architectural history of the building guided the design of the hotel. From its distinctive exterior, to the beauty of the dilapidated Victorian interior found inside, The Beekman is a hotel with provenance and its new interior scheme compliments this story. Enchanting Timelessness Victorian decadence meets industrial chic, the hotel tells a tale of architectural splendor. Selected works

items.title: Fortnum and Mason, Hong Kong — MBDS
items.text: Hong Kong Fortnum & Mason Inspired by the elegance and sophistication of Fortnum & Mason’s iconic Piccadilly store, MBDS helped the Royal grocers introduce their brand to Asia. Fortnum & Mason stands as a beacon of English hospitality in a burgeoning market Martin Brudnizki Blending together the original store's Georgian design influences with eastern inflections, moments of joy and innovation , the shop floor effectively contrasts against the ultra-modern external architecture. A ruby red woollen carpet flows throughout and pops against eau-de-nil walls and brings to life the innovative display items, including a fresh pass, tea counter and whimsical champagne display. Ascending a sweeping staircase with hand-painted mural detailing by Melissa White, guests will arrive at 181 Restaurant. The restaurant is filled with natural light, thanks to fully-glazed windows and a soft colour palette of pale green which tones effortlessly against a striking cream and gold veined marble at the bar . Pops of burnt orange leather and a unique art collection create a sense of harmony and elegance, encouraging guests to sit back and relax. Harmonious, elegant, soothing Burnt orange leather accents and unique art foster elegance and harmony, inviting guests into tranquil relaxation. Selected works

items.title: Mr C, Miami — MBDS
items.text: Miami Mr. C Capturing the timeless charm of Italy’s iconic coastal style, Mr. C Coconut Grove is an elegant and glamorous destination evoking Italy’s golden era from the Cipriani family. The interiors have been inspired by the honesty and materiality of a classic yacht. Martin Brudnizki Bellini Restaurant and Bar sits on the fifth floor of the hotel with floor to ceiling windows taking in the views across Coconut Grove Harbour and the ocean beyond. Anchoring the space to its location, a terrazzo floor spreads across both areas and elegantly combines with the high gloss limed oak panelling and bar. Nautical elements mix with typically Venetian design, as a blue and white stripe features on the seating throughout the scheme, while above sit Murano glass chandeliers – ultimately channelling the feeling of a stylish Italian yacht. Vintage Coastal Luxury Mr. C embodies Italy's golden era charm with yacht-inspired, mid-century interiors and elegant glamour. Selected works

items.title: Scott’s, London — MBDS
items.text: London Scott’s Located on Mount Street, Scott’s is a 130 cover restaurant of great provenance and indisputable style. Restoring Scott's, antique charm with functional updates, without altering its unique atmosphere. Martin Brudnizki A timber panelled dining room with burgundy leather banquettes and dining chairs, silver leaf mirrored screens and a marble top with stingray fronted bar was designed. The walls are adorned with artwork from some of today’s most celebrated British artists , including Michael Landy and Gary Hume. A specific collaboration with Patrice Butler to create a bespoke chandelier was also included in the design. Further to this Amanda Levete collaborated with the Studio to design a modern crustacean display and vanity units. Selected works

items.title: Baurs, Zurich — MBDS
items.text: Zurich Baurs Resplendent in its sophistication, the Baur au Lac hotel's deluxe brasserie unfolds as an architectural marvel. Imposing elegance meets culinary artistry in Baur au Lac's brasserie, a symphony of luxury and gastronomy. Martin Brudnizki This opulent space manages to strike a perfect balance between imposing grandeur and chic elegance, paying homage to the esteemed reputation of the renowned hotel. Every detail within the brasserie speaks volumes about its high-caliber design aesthetic. Gracefully marrying classic elements with modern accents, the interiors exude an air of timeless luxury. The lavish use of quality materials and the subtly thoughtful lighting enhance the ambiance, encapsulating the essence of fine dining. With a strong emphasis on interior design, the Baur au Lac's brasserie is not just a dining venue; it's an experience that engages all senses, establishing the space as a paragon of fine dining. Selected works

Through a bi-monthly newsletter with interviews, photo essays, product highlights and program collaborations, LONGVIEW connected Supernaturegroup with its extended community both in-person and online through social media and content. items.title: CORNER market — ELEVINE | studio
items.text: curation event production Corner Market CORNER market has become an ever expanding community of event creators, artists and makers, organized and curated by Elevine Berge. It first came together as a nomadic showroom, filling a long empty storefront on a corner in our Brooklyn neighborhood for a few days in 2019. Committed to a playful and inclusive approach to the combination of art exhibition, an immersive space of vintage furniture clothing and showcasing new design and craft, we popped up again in another empty space in the early spring of 2020, and then again and again when a time and space has feels right. Low budget and high energy, CORNER market wishes to exist outside of the now all too familiar exploitation of creatives that we find embraced by the real estate market through the “pop-up” culture. I believe in the importance of filling the many vacant storefront in all neighborhoods with local young makers, artists and performers, and my goal with CORNER market has been to keep pushing and contributing to making these spaces available at a low cost to creation, culture and life. galay studios at the most recent CORNER market, September 2024. items.title: Blinds or Curtains for Room: Which Is Better? - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: Blinds or Curtains for Room: Which Is Better? - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content Blinds or Curtains for Room: Which Is Better? Interior Design ON September 22, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A living room that gets full afternoon sun through an uncovered west-facing window doesn’t have a decorating problem. It has a glare problem, and no amount of fabric shopping fixes that until someone names it first. That’s where I start every curtains vs. blinds question a client brings me: not with color or texture, but with what the window actually has to do on an ordinary day. Can a neighbor see in? Does the sun hit a desk by 3pm? Does the bedroom need to go fully dark by 10pm? Those three questions usually narrow the choice faster than an hour in a showroom. The short version: blinds win when a window needs adjusting more than once a day, for glare, for privacy, or both. Curtains win when the room needs fuller coverage, real darkness, or more softness than a set of slats can give it. Neither wins across a whole house. In plenty of the rooms I’ve worked on, the right answer was both, with each layer doing one clear job. Where Blinds and Curtains Actually Win Treat this as a first pass, not a final answer. I’ve put curtains in a kitchen and blinds in a formal dining room when the light and the layout called for it, so use the table below to start narrowing, then check the specifics further down before you buy anything. Factor Blinds Curtains Daylight control Precise, slat by slat Broad open, partial, or fully closed Daytime privacy Easy to adjust in seconds Depends on fabric weight and weave Night privacy Good when fully closed Strong with an opaque or lined panel Room darkening Depends on fit at the frame Strong with proper lining and width Cleaning Wiped or dusted slat by slat Vacuumed, washed, or dry cleaned Space required Compact, mounts on the frame Needs wall space and stack-back room Humid rooms Several suitable materials Usually the less practical choice Visual effect Structured, close to the architecture Softer, more noticeable in the room I’d treat this table as a shortlist, not a rulebook. The same living room might take curtains in one house and blinds in another, because orientation, furniture, and privacy needs are rarely identical from one address to the next. The Differences That Actually Change How You Live With the Window This is where the real decision happens. Rather than asking which option is generally better, I compare how each one handles the specific problem sitting at your window. 1. Light Control and Glare Blinds give finer control because a 2-inch slat can be tilted to redirect daylight without shutting the window off entirely. That matters most beside a desk, a television, or a reading chair, anywhere glare shifts as the sun moves across the sky. Curtains work in bigger steps: open, partly drawn, or fully closed. A sheer panel softens bright daylight, but it doesn’t aim it the way a tilted slat does. On a window I’m adjusting several times a day, I reach for a blind almost every time. 2. Privacy During the Day and After Dark Privacy changes once the sun goes down. A tilted blind can block a direct sightline from a sidewalk or shared driveway while still letting daylight through, which is why I default to blinds in ground-floor, street-facing rooms, especially when you consider how homes balance privacy with the rest of the floor plan. Sheer curtains behave differently. They soften a daytime view, but interior lighting after dark can throw a clear silhouette onto the fabric. Before ordering a

items.text: 21 Dining Room Paint Colors for Every Style and Space - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content 21 Dining Room Paint Colors for Every Style and Space Interior Design ON September 21, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Quick answer: The best dining room paint colors range from warm whites and flexible greiges to sage, navy, terracotta, burgundy, and deep green. Choose the color according to your room’s natural and artificial light, flooring, dining furniture, adjoining spaces, and how formal or relaxed you want the room to feel. Choosing a dining room color gets complicated fast. A shade can look warm on a sample card, cooler beside the flooring, and almost completely different once the chandelier comes on at night. I pay more attention to those changes than to whichever color happens to be trending. The wall has to work with the dining table, flooring, upholstery, trim, and light already in the room. The dining room paint colors below cover quiet neutrals, earthy tones, softer colors, and richer shades. Each idea includes the type of room it suits, the design styles it supports , materials to pair with it, and a paint direction worth sampling before committing. How to Choose a Dining Room Paint Color I would not start with a paint chart. Start with the things you are not planning to replace. Flooring, the dining table, built-ins, stone, trim, and adjoining rooms should narrow the color family before individual shades come into the picture. Room Factor What to Check Why It Matters Natural light Direction and amount of daylight Changes how warm, cool, pale, or saturated paint appears Evening light Bulbs, chandelier, sconces Dining rooms often look most important after sunset Flooring Wood, tile, stone, carpet Establishes a major undertone Furniture Table, chairs, sideboard Determines how much contrast the walls need Adjoining rooms Kitchen, hallway, living room Helps connected spaces feel intentional Room scale Size, ceiling, windows Affects how much visual weight a color can carry One thing I always do before approving a color is place the sample beside the floor and dining table. Judging paint against an empty white wall tells you very little about how the finished room will actually work. Dining Room Paint Colors Worth Trying The goal is not to find one universally “best” shade. Each of these colors solves a different design problem, so start with what your dining room is missing. 1. Warm White for an Airy Room Warm white is useful when a dining room needs brightness without the sharpness of a blue-based white. Its subtle warmth works particularly well around timber, woven materials, linen, and traditional millwork. Layering a mix of surface textures like these gives the room depth even with a quiet wall color. Best room: Small, shaded, or open-plan dining room Best style: Coastal, farmhouse, traditional, organic modern Pairs with: Oak, walnut, linen, warm stone, brass Paint example: Sherwin-Williams currently features Alabaster SW 7008 in its dining-room inspiration gallery. 2. Sage Green for Natural Calm Sage introduces obvious color without demanding that every other element in the room coordinate around it. That is why I like it for everyday dining rooms where wood, plants, fabric, and pottery already bring several natural tones into the space. Best room: Casual or naturally bright dining room Best style: Farmhouse, cottage, organic modern Pairs with: Oak, cream, linen, black, aged brass Paint example: Little Greene shows Sage Green in both classic and contemporary dining spaces. 3. items.title: 15 Modern Traditional Interior Design Ideas & Tips - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: 15 Modern Traditional Interior Design Ideas & Tips - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content 15 Modern Traditional Interior Design Ideas & Tips Interior Design ON September 17, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A living room where the sofa, the rug, the side tables, and the artwork all arrived from the same delivery truck reads like a showroom floor, not a lived-in home. That is the real problem modern traditional interior design solves. It lets classic architecture, dark wood, and inherited furniture keep their worn edges, while cleaner-lined new pieces keep the room from tipping into a period set. I have reworked enough traditional rooms to know the fix is rarely a full gut. Most of the time the molding, the mantel, or the good chair someone’s grandmother left behind is already doing its job. What is usually missing is restraint on the new side of the room, and a willingness to let the old pieces look their age instead of refinishing them into submission. What Defines Modern Traditional Interior Design? Modern traditional interior design combines classic character with cleaner, more relaxed choices . The strongest rooms do not feel split between old and new. Both styles support each other through furniture, finishes, and architectural details, instead of competing for attention. Common features include: Classic details: molding, vintage rugs, curved furniture, or dark wood Modern contrast: simple silhouettes, cleaner lighting, and contemporary art Natural materials: wood, stone, linen, wool, and aged metal Collected feel: pieces from different periods instead of matching sets The best versions I’ve seen feel layered over time, with enough contrast to keep the room interesting without making it feel busy. It’s one entry in a much broader style of how homes get decorated, and it sits closer to traditional than most people expect. Get The Proportions Right Before You Buy Anything New Before any of the fifteen ideas below will look intentional, a few measurements need to be right. This is the part most rooms get wrong, and it has nothing to do with taste. Hang curtain rods 4 to 6 inches above the window frame, or closer to the ceiling if there is room for it. Hanging curtains higher and wider than the window frame is what makes a ceiling read as taller and a window read as larger. If your ceiling allows it, treat that extra height as free square footage for the room’s proportions, not an optional upgrade. Size your rug to the seating, not the room. In a living room where the sofa sits against a wall, I recommend a rug in the 7×9 to 8×10 range so the front legs of the sofa and any chairs actually sit on it. A rug that only reaches the coffee table leaves the furniture looking like it’s floating, which undercuts every other decision in the room, a mistake that shows up constantly in compact living spaces trying to stretch a small footprint wall. Pro Tip: In a room under about 150 square feet, give yourself one antique scale piece and one patterned textile, then stop. A small room with three “statement” pieces competing for attention reads as cluttered no matter how good each piece is on its own. Modern Traditional Interior Design Ideas With the proportions settled, the ideas below are where the actual character comes from. Each one uses contrast, material, or restraint differently, so pick the two or three that fit the architecture you already have rather than trying to use all of them in one room. 1. items.title: Japandi Interior Design: How to Bring the Look Home
items.text: Japandi Interior Design: How to Bring the Look Home Skip to content Japandi Interior Design: How to Bring the Look Home Interior Design ON September 14, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Your Japandi interior design search probably started the same way mine always does. You save a dozen photos of the same warm sofa and clean shelf, then stand in your own living room feeling stuck. The photos make sense until you try to copy them, and the room still feels wrong somehow. That gap between the photo and your actual space is the real problem, not a lack of taste. I built this guide to close that gap room by room, with the exact measurements, furniture swaps, and budget order that make the style hold up in a real home. By the end, you’ll know exactly where to start and what to skip. Cost Note: Figures in this are estimates based on national averages for furniture and materials. Actual costs vary by region, retailer, and materials used. Get at least three quotes before committing to any purchase or project above $1,000. What Japandi Interior Design Actually Means Japandi interior design blends Japanese restraint with Scandinavian warmth, and the easiest way to understand it is through the two ideas it borrows from. The style pairs wabi-sabi, the Japanese idea of finding beauty in a natural, slightly imperfect finish , with hygge, the Scandinavian idea of a warm and settled kind of comfort. Design writers covering the style point to that same pairing as the reason it reads as calm instead of bare. In practice, that means a room built around a small number of natural materials, wood, linen, wool, stone, clay, rather than a room built around decoration. Low furniture, warm neutral walls, and one or two considered plants do more work than a shelf full of objects. The Layout Rules That Actually Make a Room Read as Japandi Before you buy a single throw pillow, the room’s bones have to work. According to the National Kitchen and Bath Association’s planning guidelines, a main walkway should stay at least 30 to 36 inches wide, and a sofa should sit 14 to 18 inches from a coffee table. Those numbers do not change because a room is styled in a certain way. If the path through your living room is 20 inches wide, no amount of linen and ceramic will make it feel calm. Furniture height matters just as much as clearance. Platform beds and low-profile sofas common to this style typically sit several inches lower than standard pieces, often in the 14 to 17 inch range rather than the usual 18 or so inches at the seat. In my own layouts, I try to keep a sofa under about three-quarters of the wall it sits against. Past that, a room starts to feel like the furniture is doing the deciding, not you. Pro Tip: Group decor in odd numbers, one vase, three books, and leave at least one surface in every room visibly clear. A single empty shelf reads as intentional. A single empty room reads as unfinished. Two Ways to Get There, Depending on Your Budget and Timeline There is more than one honest path into this look, and they trade off differently. Approach Typical Cost Time to See a Difference Trade-off Work with what you own $150 to $400 A weekend Textiles and small decor shift the mood, but a tall sofa or bulky bed frame still reads as the wrong style underneath it Replace the anchor piece $800 to $2,500+ Several weeks to a season Bigger upfront spend, but the low profile and proportion of a new sofa or bed frame does more than any amount of styling Most rooms end up somewhere between the two: one new anchor piece, everything else worked in slowly. items.text: 21 Small Bathroom Walk-In Shower Ideas Worth Considering - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content 21 Small Bathroom Walk-In Shower Ideas Worth Considering Functional Spaces ON September 22, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A 5-foot by 8-foot bathroom with a swinging door and a floor-mounted vanity does not have a shower problem. It has a clearance problem, and that is the first thing I check before sketching a single small bathroom walk-in shower idea on paper. What matters most is how the shower sits next to the vanity, toilet, doorway, and the path you use every day. As an interior designer, I look at circulation before finishes. I would rather adjust a vanity depth or rethink an awkward corner than force a shower into the wrong spot. The strongest small bathroom walk-in shower ideas use the existing room shape to build a layout that feels comfortable instead of crowded. A narrow bath may suit a full-width shower, while a square room often works better with a corner setup. The ideas ahead cover layout, finish, and space-saving details that hold up once the tile is set and the water is running. What Makes a Walk-In Shower Work in a Small Bathroom? A successful walk-in shower fits the bathroom as a whole, not just the available corner. Enough space around nearby fixtures matters just as much as the shower dimensions. Keep proportions balanced: Avoid making the shower so large that the vanity or toilet feels squeezed. Protect the walking path: The shower entrance should not interfere with the bathroom door or other fixtures. Once you know how shower sizing works for a given footprint, the National Kitchen and Bath Association’s recommendation of at least 30 inches of clear floor space in front of any fixture, well above the 21-inch code minimum, is the number I hold every layout to. Define the wet area: Use a glass panel, half wall, or existing walls to contain water without over-enclosing the room. Use the walls: Built-in niches and slim ledges reduce the need for bulky shower organizers. Keep boundaries simple: Fewer partitions help the layout stay easy to read and use. Choose the Shower Layout Before the Style Before choosing tile or fixtures, decide where the shower makes the most sense. The room shape and existing plumbing usually point toward the most practical position. The table below shows how common small-bathroom conditions can guide the most practical shower placement. Bathroom Condition Shower Position Why It Works Long and narrow Across the back wall Keeps one clear route through the room Small square Corner Leaves more usable floor in the center Existing alcove Inside the recess Uses walls already in place Bathtub remodel Existing tub footprint Avoids unnecessary layout changes Awkward shape Angled or custom corner Uses space that is difficult to furnish Long room with tub Shared wet zone Keeps both a shower and bathtub The goal is to choose the position that interferes least with everyday movement. Once that is settled, glass, tile, color, and storage become much easier to plan. Small Bathroom Walk-In Shower Ideas These ideas approach a small walk-in shower from different angles: room shape, enclosure, storage, seating, tile, color, and overall style. The goal is not to make every bathroom look alike, but to show practical ways different compact spaces can handle a walk-in shower. 1. Run the Shower Across the Back Wall In long bathrooms, I often put the shower across the short back wall instead of squeezing it along one side. It gives the shower usable width while keeping the vanity and toilet along a

items.title: Walk-In Shower Dimensions: A Practical Size Guide - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: Walk-In Shower Dimensions: A Practical Size Guide - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content Walk-In Shower Dimensions: A Practical Size Guide Functional Spaces ON September 19, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Quick Answer: Common walk-in shower dimensions start around 36 x 36 inches, while 36 x 48 inches gives one person more comfortable movement. Larger 48-inch or 60-inch layouts work better for benches, open entries, or extra fixtures. The best size depends on usable standing room, bathroom circulation, glass placement, and the shower entry. A shower can fit neatly on a floor plan and still feel wrong once the bathroom is built. I pay almost as much attention to the space around the shower as I do to it interior dimensions. The right walk-in shower dimensions depend on more than width and depth. Entry position, nearby fixtures, seating, glass, and the amount of clear standing room all affect how comfortable the shower feels. Start with the bathroom layout first. Then decide how much space the shower can reasonably take without squeezing the vanity, toilet, doorway, or main walking path. Standard Walk-In Shower Dimensions For everyday use, I usually find 36 x 48 inches a more forgiving starting point when the room allows it. Larger layouts make sense when you are replacing a tub, adding a bench, planning an open entry, or accommodating additional fixtures. These common walk-in shower dimensions offer a practical starting point for comparing space, comfort, and layout needs before final planning. Shower Size Best For Planning Note 36 x 36 in. Compact bathrooms Works for one person but leaves little extra floor area 36 x 42 in. Small one-person shower Adds useful depth without taking much more width 36 x 48 in. Comfortable daily use Gives better movement while remaining manageable in many bathrooms 48 x 48 in. Roomier square layout Offers more turning and fixture space 60 x 30 in. Tub replacement Can use the length of an existing five-foot alcove 60 x 36 to 42 in. Larger shower or seating Gives more flexibility for a bench or additional fixtures Treat these as planning dimensions rather than one universal residential code chart. Local requirements, finished dimensions, and the shower configuration still affect what will work. How To Choose The Right Shower Size Start with the bathroom, not the shower. Adding six inches inside the enclosure may sound worthwhile, but not if it leaves an awkward squeeze between the shower opening and vanity. The same principle matters when planning bathroom circulation and layout , because the shower has to work with every fixture around it. Before settling on a size: Measure The Available Footprint: Find the maximum width and depth without crowding the toilet, vanity, door, or walking path. Plan The Entry: Check that you can step in comfortably after glass and hardware are installed. Allow For Finished Walls: Backer board, waterproofing, mortar, and tile reduce the usable interior dimensions. Mark Fixture Locations: Position the showerhead, controls, handheld, niches, and ledges before judging the available standing space. Account For Seating: A bench can remove much more usable floor area than it appears to on a plan. Check Existing Plumbing: Reusing practical drain and supply locations may simplify a remodel. A 36 x 48-inch shower can therefore feel smaller than expected once everything is installed. I would protect comfortable bathroom circulation first.
